pages.title: Shock physiology, emergency response, and First Aid boundaries
pages.text: Electrical injury is controlled first by removing exposure, not by rushing to touch the injured person. Shock severity depends on current magnitude, the path through the body, contact duration, frequency, skin/contact condition, and the person’s condition. Effects can range from pain and involuntary muscle contraction to burns, respiratory arrest, dangerous heart rhythms, and death. A person may be unable to release an energized conductor. If an electrical contact occurs, do not become a second victim: do not touch the person while the source may still be energized. Call emergency services, have the source disconnected by a safe method within your training and site procedure, and use CPR, an AED, bleeding/burn care, or other First Aid only to the level you are trained and authorized to provide. Electrical injury can involve hidden internal damage even when skin injury looks small, so professional medical evaluation can be necessary. For an untrained worker the correct competence is recognition and escalation: identify the emergency, keep others away, call for help, remove energy only when that can be done safely, and follow dispatcher/site instructions. This course does not authorize energized rescue or substitute for hands-on First Aid/CPR/AED training.

pages.title: NEC awareness, overcurrent protection, and lockout/tagout
pages.text: The National Electrical Code (NFPA 70) is primarily an installation code: it addresses how electrical systems and equipment are installed so hazards are controlled. It is not a substitute for employer safe-work procedures or the energized-work rules that apply to a technician’s task. A technician therefore follows the applicable code, listing/labeling and manufacturer instructions, and also follows workplace safety procedures. Fuses and circuit breakers protect conductors and equipment from excessive current. Replacement means matching the required device type, voltage rating, current rating, and interrupting capability; a slow-blow/time-delay fuse and a fast-acting fuse can behave very differently during normal inrush. Never bypass a protective device or substitute a larger rating merely to stop nuisance opening. Lockout/tagout controls hazardous energy before servicing: identify energy sources, shut down, isolate them, apply the authorized lock/tag, control stored energy, and verify the de-energized/zero-energy condition before work. A software Stop button, open control contact, or dark display is not proof of isolation. Only people trained and authorized under the employer’s energy-control program perform the lockout steps that require that authorization.

pages.title: ESD, technician tool hazards, and PPE
pages.text: Electrostatic discharge is a rapid transfer of charge caused by a voltage difference. A discharge too small to feel can still puncture or weaken semiconductor junctions, especially CMOS inputs. At an approved de-energized ESD workstation, control static with a verified dissipative mat, approved wrist strap/grounding system, grounded tools where specified, antistatic packaging, and handling that avoids touching contacts. ESD controls are not permission to connect yourself to hazardous energized equipment; site procedures govern when straps may be worn. Technician hazards also include damaged insulation, cracked probes, wrong meter category/rating, metal jewelry, hot soldering tools, sharp leads, batteries capable of high fault current, rotating mechanisms, and stored energy in capacitors. PPE is chosen from the actual hazard assessment: eye protection, gloves, arc-rated clothing, hearing protection, footwear, or other equipment may be required by the task and workplace. PPE is a layer of protection, not a reason to skip de-energization, guarding, isolation, correct tools, or safe distance.

pages.title: RF exposure and fiber-optic hazards
pages.text: RF exposure risk depends on frequency, transmitter power, antenna gain, duty cycle, distance, exposure duration, and whether the exposure is occupational/controlled or general/uncontrolled. Maximum Permissible Exposure (MPE) limits are therefore not one universal distance or power number. A technician follows the organization’s RF-safety program, posted boundaries, lockout/interlock rules, and the applicable FCC/OSHA/ANSI method; never defeat an interlock, stand in a restricted antenna field, or assume a transmitter is safe because the RF cannot be seen. Fiber systems create different hazards. Active fibers can carry invisible infrared light that can injure the eye, and cleaving/splicing creates tiny glass shards that can penetrate skin or eyes. Never look into a fiber or connector to see whether it is live; use a rated optical test instrument and verify the source state. Wear appropriate eye protection, keep food/drink away, cap unused ends, collect scraps in a dedicated sharps container, and clean the work area. RF and fiber both require recognizing invisible hazards, but the mechanisms and controls are different.

pages.title: Ladders, service vehicles, and fire classes
pages.text: A ladder is equipment that must be selected and inspected for the task. Check feet, rails, rungs, locks and labels; set it on a stable surface, maintain required angle/securement for the ladder type, keep three-point control while climbing, and do not overreach. Around electrical hazards, follow the workplace rule for nonconductive ladders and minimum approach boundaries. Service vehicles add stored and moving hazards: secure ladders, batteries, tools and heavy equipment against sudden stops; preserve the driver’s view; use approved racks/tie-downs; and keep loose objects from becoming projectiles. Fire classes describe the fuel involved: A is ordinary combustibles, B flammable liquids/gases, C energized electrical equipment, D combustible metals, and K cooking oils/fats. Extinguishers are selected for the fuel and site plan. De-energizing can change the electrical aspect of a Class C incident, but a technician should use the approved extinguisher and emergency procedure and attempt firefighting only when trained, the fire is incipient/small, an escape path is maintained, and site policy permits it.

pages.title: From charge and energy to voltage and current
pages.text: Start with charge rather than the formula triangle. Electric charge is a property of matter measured in coulombs. Current is the rate at which charge passes a point: one ampere is one coulomb per second. Voltage is not a substance moving through a wire; it is an electrical potential difference between two points, meaning a difference in energy per unit charge. A source can create that difference, and a closed conductive path allows charge to move. Resistance describes how strongly a component opposes that current for a given applied voltage. This picture explains why voltage is measured across two points while current is measured through a path. It also explains open and short circuits: an open breaks the current path; a short creates an unintended low-resistance path that can allow dangerously high current.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

pages.title: The technician’s first measurement happens before power
pages.text: Inspect source polarity, component orientation, exposed conductors, connector direction, and likely short paths. With power disconnected, continuity or resistance checks can reveal a rail-to-ground short. Set the supply voltage to the intended value and begin with a conservative current limit. State a stop condition such as “remove power if current immediately reaches the limit, a part heats, smoke appears, or the measured rail is outside tolerance.” This turns safety into a repeatable process instead of a vague promise to be careful.
pages.remember: Inspect → predict → limit → power → observe → stop if the evidence violates the plan.
pages.sourceLesson: Safe bench setup, prediction, and measurement

pages.title: A safe bench begins before power is applied
pages.text: Bench work is controlled experimentation. Before energizing a circuit, identify the exact source, its maximum voltage/current capability, the circuit reference, polarized parts, expected current, and the point at which you will stop. Inspect the board for loose conductors, reversed electrolytics or diodes, conductive debris, and incorrect wiring. Set the bench supply voltage first with the output disabled, set a conservative current limit, and know which meter jacks and modes are active. The purpose of this sequence is not paperwork; it prevents a simple setup error from becoming a damaged board, blown meter fuse, or misleading measurement.
pages.sourceLesson: Safe bench setup, prediction, and measurement

pages.title: Recognize the safety rules that surround bench work
pages.text: Shock can trigger involuntary muscle contraction, so a person may be unable to release an energized conductor; never touch the person while the source remains energized. Call emergency services and remove energy only by a safe, trained method. A fuse is a protective component, not a convenient wire: replace it only with the specified type, voltage rating, current rating, and interrupting capability. For CMOS handling, use the approved grounded ESD mat and wrist strap only at a verified de-energized ESD station. Lockout/tagout is more than pressing Stop: hazardous energy is isolated, locked, identified, and verified according to the employer’s procedure. In the United States, energized electrical equipment is associated with Class C fire involvement; use the site’s approved extinguisher and emergency plan, never water. These are recognition rules for CETa preparation—not authorization to perform energized rescue, mains service, fire response, or workplace lockout without required training.
pages.remember: De-energize and escalate. Match protective devices exactly. Control static at an approved station. Never improvise around shock, fire, or hazardous energy.
pages.sourceLesson: Safe bench setup, prediction, and measurement

pages.title: Technician application: bench safety, ESD, pre-power control, and hazard logging
pages.text: A technician-controlled bench begins before energizing: identify source voltage/current capability, set a conservative current limit, verify polarity and connector orientation, inspect for shorts/exposed conductors, select the correct DMM mode/jack, establish an explicit stop condition, and document the setup. ESD controls protect semiconductors but do not substitute for shock/energy controls. Soldering/rework adds eye protection, ventilation, hot-tool and cutting/crimp hazards. The decision boundary is part of competence: isolated current-limited low-voltage work can be appropriate for this course, while unknown energized equipment, mains, high-energy batteries or charged high-voltage capacitors require trained/qualified procedures. C1.6 is explicit: if a safety/setup hazard is discovered, stop the test, record the condition and risk, correct it, independently verify the safe state/settings, record the corrective action, and only then continue under the required authorization.
pages.sourceLesson: Safe bench setup, prediction, and measurement

pages.title: ESD damage can be latent and invisible
pages.text: Static charge can reach damaging voltage without a sensation. Grounded dissipative mats, correctly connected wrist straps, antistatic packaging, controlled handling, and common-point grounding reduce potential differences. A strap is not used for hazardous energized work. ESD control protects components; electrical safety protects people, and the controls must not be confused.
pages.remember: Protect device, person, and process with the right control for each hazard.
pages.sourceLesson: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

pages.title: ESD control is specific to the work state
pages.text: At a suitable de-energized ESD workstation, use approved grounding systems, dissipative surfaces, packaging, and handling practices. An ESD wrist strap is not permission to connect yourself to hazardous energized circuitry. Workmanship control also includes ventilation/fume management, eye protection, hot-tool handling, and lead/solder hygiene. Physical skill claims require physical evidence; a virtual inspection can teach defect recognition but cannot prove hand technique, heat control, or actual joint quality.
pages.sourceLesson: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

examples.title: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

detail.problem: A 9 V source is connected across a 1.0 kΩ resistor. Find current and resistor power.
steps: Convert 1.0 kΩ to 1,000 Ω.
A common 0.25 W resistor has margin because 0.081 W is well below 0.25 W.
detail.answer: 9 mA and 81 mW.
detail.transfer: If the resistance were accidentally 100 Ω, current and power would each be ten times larger; that is why the value and current limit are checked before power-up.

examples.title: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

detail.problem: A 12 V source feeds a 680 ohm resistor. Predict current and resistor power, then decide whether a 1/8 W resistor is suitable.
steps: Current: I = 12 V / 680 ohm = 0.01765 A, about 17.6 mA.
A 1/8 W resistor is rated 0.125 W, below the predicted dissipation.
Choose a higher power rating and leave reasonable thermal margin rather than operating at the edge.
detail.answer: About 17.6 mA and 0.212 W; a 1/8 W resistor is not suitable.
detail.meaning: The arithmetic predicts not just a value but whether a physical component is safe to use.

examples.title: Safe bench setup, prediction, and measurement

detail.problem: You are about to power a 5 V LED circuit. The supply shows 5.0 V and a 20 mA limit; the meter lead remains in the A jack from yesterday.
steps: Do not connect the meter across the circuit.
Move the lead to the voltage/ohms jack and select DC volts if measuring voltage.
Inspect LED polarity and series resistor; check rail-to-ground resistance with power off.
State the stop condition, then power while watching supply current.
detail.answer: Correct the meter configuration before power. A current-jack meter across the rail could short it.
detail.transfer: The same pre-power discipline is used during PCB bring-up, where current consumption is an early fault signal.

examples.title: Safe bench setup, prediction, and measurement

detail.problem: A 5 V development board is expected to draw 35-60 mA at idle. On first power with a 100 mA current limit, the supply enters CC mode at 100 mA and the output falls to 1.2 V.
steps: The low rail is not evidence of a weak 5 V supply; CC mode says the load is demanding more than the set limit.
Disable the output rather than raising the limit.
Perform power-off inspection and rail-to-ground resistance checks; compare with board documentation if available.
Look for polarity errors, solder bridges, wrong connector orientation, or a shorted peripheral before another controlled power attempt.
detail.answer: Stop and investigate the load/short path. Do not raise the current limit merely to make the rail reach 5 V.
detail.meaning: Supply mode is part of the measurement. It tells you whether voltage or current is the controlled quantity.

examples.title: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

detail.problem: A through-hole joint forms a dull ball around the lead and does not spread over the pad.
steps: This suggests inadequate wetting, contamination, insufficient heat transfer, or movement.
Inspect tip condition, surface cleanliness, flux, temperature, and whether pad and lead were heated together.
Reflow with controlled heat only if the pad is intact and the process is safe.
Inspect, continuity-check, and functionally verify afterward.
detail.answer: Treat the shape as evidence of poor wetting; correct the process, then verify electrically.
detail.transfer: The same diagnostic habit separates symptom from cause in electronics faults.

guided.text: A 3.3 V source is applied to 1.5 kOhm. Calculate current, then state whether 1 mA or 10 mA is the more sensible mental estimate before calculating.
A resistor carries 20 mA with 5 V across it. Find resistance and power. Keep units through every step.
Sketch a source, resistor, return path, and reference node. Mark where a voltmeter connects and where an ammeter would have to be inserted.
Write a pre-power checklist for a 3.3 V sensor breakout connected to a microcontroller board. Include voltage compatibility, polarity, ground reference, current limit, and expected idle current.
For a DMM with leads currently in COM and A jacks, describe exactly what must change before measuring 3.3 V across a rail.
A board draws 18 mA normally. The supply limit is 25 mA and the board enters CC mode after a new cable is connected. List two plausible setup causes and one safe test that distinguishes them.

teachBack: Explain voltage, current, resistance, and power to a new technician without using a formula triangle. Then use one resistor example to show how the four quantities connect and why a power rating matters.

Teach a new lab partner how to power an unfamiliar low-voltage board safely. Explain CV versus CC behavior, meter-jack risk, what you inspect before power, and the observation that would make you stop immediately.

Explain what creates a reliable solder joint, why solder wick works, what makes BGA/pad repair different from simple through-hole rework, and why ESD/physical-skill claims require real procedures and evidence.

questions.prompt: Why can a shock prevent someone from releasing a live conductor?
choices: Current can trigger involuntary muscle contraction.
The skin always becomes a perfect insulator.
The conductor loses all voltage on contact.
Only the person's conscious grip can hold the conductor.
questions.explanation: Shock can disrupt muscle control as well as breathing and heart rhythm. Never approach a live contact as a safe experiment.

questions.prompt: A device specifies a particular fuse type and current rating. What is the appropriate replacement approach?
choices: Use the specified type and ratings, including adequate voltage and interrupting ratings.
Use any fuse that fits if its current rating is higher.
Bridge the holder with wire during normal use.
questions.explanation: Physical fit is insufficient. Current, operating characteristic, voltage and interrupting capability are part of fuse selection.

questions.prompt: Which practice reduces ESD risk when handling an unpowered CMOS board at an approved ESD bench?
choices: Use the bench's tested grounding and ESD handling procedure.
Carry the board loose in ordinary plastic packaging.
Rub the board with a dry synthetic cloth.
Hold exposed pins to equalize them with a nearby mains outlet.
questions.explanation: ESD controls manage charge differences. They do not authorize work on energized hazardous circuits.

questions.prompt: A machine is switched off before service. Why is its ordinary Stop button insufficient proof of energy isolation?
choices: Power could return, and stored or other energy sources may remain.
A Stop button always physically disconnects every energy source.
Stored energy disappears instantly when motion stops.
Lockout is only about labeling the repair date.
questions.explanation: Follow the applicable authorized isolation and verification procedure. A control command is different from verified isolation.

questions.prompt: In the US fire classification system, which class identifies energized electrical equipment involvement?
questions.explanation: Class C concerns energized electrical equipment. Response and extinguisher selection require appropriate training and site procedures.

pages.title: Atoms, charge, current, voltage, resistance, and uses of electricity
pages.text: Atoms contain positively charged protons, neutral neutrons, and negatively charged electrons. Electronics is primarily concerned with how charge carriers move or are redistributed in materials. One coulomb is a quantity of charge; one ampere is one coulomb per second. Current is therefore a rate of charge flow, while voltage is energy difference per unit charge between two points. Resistance describes how strongly a material/device opposes current for a given applied voltage. These terms are not interchangeable: a 5 V source can exist with nearly zero current when the circuit is open, and a low resistance can allow very large current if the source can supply it. Electrical energy is used for heating, light, motion, computation, communication, sensing, storage and conversion. A technician uses the same quantities whether the device is a simple resistor circuit or an embedded board: identify the source/reference, predict current paths, check voltage differences, and verify power/rating limits.

pages.title: From charge and energy to voltage and current
pages.text: Start with charge rather than the formula triangle. Electric charge is a property of matter measured in coulombs. Current is the rate at which charge passes a point: one ampere is one coulomb per second. Voltage is not a substance moving through a wire; it is an electrical potential difference between two points, meaning a difference in energy per unit charge. A source can create that difference, and a closed conductive path allows charge to move. Resistance describes how strongly a component opposes that current for a given applied voltage. This picture explains why voltage is measured across two points while current is measured through a path. It also explains open and short circuits: an open breaks the current path; a short creates an unintended low-resistance path that can allow dangerously high current.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

pages.title: A circuit is a complete path, not a pile of parts
pages.text: Current is the rate at which charge passes a point; its unit is the ampere. Voltage is energy difference per unit charge between two points; it is never a property of one unreferenced point. Resistance describes how strongly an element opposes current for a given voltage. Power is the rate of energy transfer. A source, conductors, and a load must form a closed path before steady current can flow. An open breaks that path. A short creates an unintended very-low-resistance path and can force destructive current.
pages.remember: Voltage is measured across two points. Current flows through a path. Resistance shapes their relationship. Power tells how fast energy is converted.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

pages.title: Core formulas, SI prefixes, NIST spelling exceptions, and scientific notation
pages.text: Technician math begins by writing the relationship with units. Core relationships include V=IR, P=VI, f=1/T, wavelength λ=v/f, XC=1/(2πfC), XL=2πfL and resonant frequency f0=1/(2π√LC), along with context-specific ratios such as transformer turns and dB. SI prefixes are powers of ten: p 10⁻¹², n 10⁻⁹, µ 10⁻⁶, m 10⁻³, k 10³, M 10⁶, G 10⁹. Prefix case matters: m is milli while M is mega. Scientific notation keeps the coefficient times 10^n and makes prefix conversion visible. NIST writing guidance includes traditional unit-name spellings such as kilohm and megohm as exceptions to simply joining a prefix name to “ohm”; symbols remain kΩ and MΩ. Correct calculations keep units through substitution and make an order-of-magnitude estimate before trusting a calculator.
pages.sourceLesson: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

pages.title: Ohm's law as a model with limits
pages.text: For an ohmic resistor over its intended operating range, voltage, current, and resistance are related by V = IR. The equation does not mean every device has constant resistance. Lamps, diodes, transistors, thermistors, motors, and semiconductor junctions can be nonlinear. Use Ohm's law when the device or circuit condition supports the model, and use a datasheet or measured characteristic when it does not. A useful habit is to predict direction and magnitude before calculating: increasing resistance at fixed voltage must reduce current; increasing voltage at fixed resistance must increase current. Then use units to catch mistakes. Five volts across two kilohms is naturally 2.5 milliamperes because volts divided by kilohms gives milliamperes.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

pages.title: Sources, AC measures, duty cycle, pulse width, Ohm’s law, and power
pages.text: Sources may be DC (battery, regulated supply, rectified/regulator output, photovoltaic or other generation) or AC (utility/alternator/signal generator). For a symmetric sine wave, peak is the maximum excursion from the reference, peak-to-peak is twice the peak, and Vrms = Vpk/√2; RMS is the DC-equivalent heating measure for a resistive load. A pulsed DC waveform alternates between levels. Pulse width is the time a pulse remains in its active state; period is the time for one full cycle; duty cycle is pulse width/period × 100%. At 1 kHz, period is 1 ms; a 250 µs high pulse has 25% duty cycle. Ohm’s law V=IR can be rearranged to I=V/R and R=V/I. Power can be found from P=VI and, for resistive cases, P=I²R or V²/R. Correct work retains units/prefixes and checks source/component ratings rather than stopping at arithmetic.
pages.sourceLesson: Series, parallel, KVL, KCL, and divider reasoning

pages.title: Power connects the math to heat and ratings
pages.text: Electrical power is P = VI. Combining it with Ohm’s law gives P = I²R and P = V²/R. Those forms answer different measurement situations, but they describe the same energy rate. A calculated 0.18 W in a 0.25 W resistor is electrically possible but leaves little margin; a technician checks rating and temperature rather than stopping at the arithmetic. Polarity marks the intended direction of voltage or current. Reversing a polarized LED, electrolytic capacitor, or supply can prevent operation or cause damage.
pages.remember: A correct voltage or current answer is incomplete until component power and polarity are safe.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

pages.title: Decibels and graphs as engineering representations
pages.text: Decibels express ratios logarithmically. For power ratios use 10 log10(P2/P1); for voltage ratios use 20 log10(V2/V1) only when the impedances are equal or the context justifies that conversion. +3 dB is about twice power, -3 dB about half power, +10 dB ten times power, and -10 dB one tenth. Absolute levels such as dBm add a reference; 0 dBm is 1 mW. Graphs reveal relationships that a single number hides: waveform plots show value versus time, frequency-response plots show gain/phase versus frequency, IV curves show device behavior, and trend plots show drift/repeatability. Always label axes, units, scale type (linear/log), reference and conditions; otherwise a graph can be technically true but misleading.
pages.sourceLesson: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

pages.title: Power, heat, and ratings
pages.text: Power connects electrical calculations to physical consequences. P = VI is the rate at which electrical energy is delivered or converted. For a resistor, combining Ohm's law gives P = I^2R and P = V^2/R. A correct current is not enough; the component must survive the resulting power and temperature. A 0.25 W resistor dissipating 0.22 W may be below its nameplate rating but has little thermal margin, especially in a hot enclosure. A technician therefore checks both the nominal calculation and the rating context. This same reasoning later appears in transistor dissipation, regulator heating, wiring limits, and power-supply current limits.

detail.meaning: The arithmetic predicts not just a value but whether a physical component is safe to use.

examples.title: Series, parallel, KVL, KCL, and divider reasoning

detail.problem: A 12 V source feeds 2 kΩ in series with 4 kΩ. Find current, both drops, and unloaded output across 4 kΩ.
steps: RT = 2 kΩ + 4 kΩ = 6 kΩ.
I = 12 V / 6 kΩ = 2 mA.
V2k = 2 mA × 2 kΩ = 4 V.
V4k = 2 mA × 4 kΩ = 8 V.
KVL check: 4 V + 8 V = 12 V.
detail.answer: 2 mA, 4 V, and 8 V.
detail.transfer: If a 4 kΩ load is attached across the lower 4 kΩ, the lower equivalent becomes 2 kΩ; the output becomes 6 V, not 8 V.

examples.title: Series, parallel, KVL, KCL, and divider reasoning

detail.problem: A 12 V divider uses 3.3 kOhm on top and 2.2 kOhm on bottom. Find unloaded Vout, then find Vout when a 2.2 kOhm load is connected from output to ground.
steps: Loaded lower leg: 2.2 kOhm || 2.2 kOhm = 1.1 kOhm.
The heavy load changes the circuit substantially; the original divider equation using 2.2 kOhm alone is no longer valid.
detail.answer: 4.8 V unloaded and 3.0 V with the 2.2 kOhm load.
detail.meaning: A connected instrument or downstream stage can become part of the network and change the value being measured.

examples.title: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

detail.problem: A 10 kΩ resistor charges a 10 µF capacitor from a 5 V step. Find τ and approximate voltage after one τ.
steps: After one τ, the capacitor has completed about 63% of the change.
After about 5τ = 0.5 s, it is near the final value.
detail.answer: τ = 0.1 s; Vc at one τ is about 3.15 V.
detail.transfer: A scope cursor can test both the predicted time and voltage on the charging curve.

pages.title: Resistor families, markings, thermistors, and potentiometers
pages.text: Fixed resistors include carbon-film, metal-film and wirewound constructions. Metal film is often chosen for stability/low noise; wirewound parts handle higher power but may have inductance; thermistors intentionally change resistance with temperature. Potentiometers have two end terminals and a movable wiper, allowing them to act as a three-terminal voltage divider; rheostats use the wiper plus one end as a variable resistance. Color bands or printed/SMD codes identify nominal value and tolerance, but the exact marking system depends on package. For a lightly loaded potentiometer, Vwiper = Vin × Rbottom/(Rtop+Rbottom), where the resistances are the two sections split by the wiper. Loading the wiper changes the ratio because the load is in parallel with one section. NTC thermistors decrease resistance as temperature increases; PTC devices increase. They appear in sensing, inrush control and protection.
pages.sourceLesson: Component families, ratings, magnetism, and machines

pages.title: A part name does not establish suitability
pages.text: Resistors require value, tolerance, power, and sometimes voltage/temperature ratings. Capacitors add capacitance, working voltage, dielectric/type, polarity, ESR, and tolerance. Inductors add inductance, current/saturation, resistance, and core behavior. Switches and relay contacts have voltage/current/load-type ratings. Read markings, then confirm with a datasheet or measurement; physical size alone is not a specification.
pages.remember: Function + electrical value + stress rating + environment + package must all fit.
pages.sourceLesson: Component families, ratings, magnetism, and machines

pages.title: Ohm’s law is a relationship, not three unrelated formulas
pages.text: For an ohmic element, V = I × R. The same relationship can be rearranged as I = V/R or R = V/I. Choose the form by naming what is known and what is unknown before touching a calculator. Keep base units consistent: volts, amperes, and ohms. A 1 kΩ resistor is 1,000 Ω; 1 mA is 0.001 A. Engineering prefixes move in factors of one thousand, so 4.7 kΩ and 2 mA are often easier to reason with directly: volts divided by kilohms gives milliamperes.
pages.remember: Write Given → Find → Relationship → Substitute with units → Sanity-check.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

pages.title: Ohm's law as a model with limits
pages.text: For an ohmic resistor over its intended operating range, voltage, current, and resistance are related by V = IR. The equation does not mean every device has constant resistance. Lamps, diodes, transistors, thermistors, motors, and semiconductor junctions can be nonlinear. Use Ohm's law when the device or circuit condition supports the model, and use a datasheet or measured characteristic when it does not. A useful habit is to predict direction and magnitude before calculating: increasing resistance at fixed voltage must reduce current; increasing voltage at fixed resistance must increase current. Then use units to catch mistakes. Five volts across two kilohms is naturally 2.5 milliamperes because volts divided by kilohms gives milliamperes.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

pages.title: Sources, AC measures, duty cycle, pulse width, Ohm’s law, and power
pages.text: Sources may be DC (battery, regulated supply, rectified/regulator output, photovoltaic or other generation) or AC (utility/alternator/signal generator). For a symmetric sine wave, peak is the maximum excursion from the reference, peak-to-peak is twice the peak, and Vrms = Vpk/√2; RMS is the DC-equivalent heating measure for a resistive load. A pulsed DC waveform alternates between levels. Pulse width is the time a pulse remains in its active state; period is the time for one full cycle; duty cycle is pulse width/period × 100%. At 1 kHz, period is 1 ms; a 250 µs high pulse has 25% duty cycle. Ohm’s law V=IR can be rearranged to I=V/R and R=V/I. Power can be found from P=VI and, for resistive cases, P=I²R or V²/R. Correct work retains units/prefixes and checks source/component ratings rather than stopping at arithmetic.
pages.sourceLesson: Series, parallel, KVL, KCL, and divider reasoning

pages.title: Power connects the math to heat and ratings
pages.text: Electrical power is P = VI. Combining it with Ohm’s law gives P = I²R and P = V²/R. Those forms answer different measurement situations, but they describe the same energy rate. A calculated 0.18 W in a 0.25 W resistor is electrically possible but leaves little margin; a technician checks rating and temperature rather than stopping at the arithmetic. Polarity marks the intended direction of voltage or current. Reversing a polarized LED, electrolytic capacitor, or supply can prevent operation or cause damage.
pages.remember: A correct voltage or current answer is incomplete until component power and polarity are safe.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

pages.title: Power, heat, and ratings
pages.text: Power connects electrical calculations to physical consequences. P = VI is the rate at which electrical energy is delivered or converted. For a resistor, combining Ohm's law gives P = I^2R and P = V^2/R. A correct current is not enough; the component must survive the resulting power and temperature. A 0.25 W resistor dissipating 0.22 W may be below its nameplate rating but has little thermal margin, especially in a hot enclosure. A technician therefore checks both the nominal calculation and the rating context. This same reasoning later appears in transistor dissipation, regulator heating, wiring limits, and power-supply current limits.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

pages.title: Component type predicts behavior and failure modes
pages.text: A resistor's construction matters: metal-film parts often offer good stability and low noise; wirewound resistors handle higher power but can introduce inductance; thermistors intentionally change resistance with temperature; potentiometers provide an adjustable divider; rheostats use an adjustable resistance path. Capacitors differ by dielectric, polarity, voltage rating, ESR, leakage, and frequency behavior. Inductors differ in core material, saturation current, winding resistance, and intended frequency. A technician uses markings and datasheets to identify not only the nominal value but the constraints that determine whether a replacement will behave correctly.
pages.sourceLesson: Component families, ratings, magnetism, and machines

pages.title: A circuit is a complete path, not a pile of parts
pages.text: Current is the rate at which charge passes a point; its unit is the ampere. Voltage is energy difference per unit charge between two points; it is never a property of one unreferenced point. Resistance describes how strongly an element opposes current for a given voltage. Power is the rate of energy transfer. A source, conductors, and a load must form a closed path before steady current can flow. An open breaks that path. A short creates an unintended very-low-resistance path and can force destructive current.
pages.remember: Voltage is measured across two points. Current flows through a path. Resistance shapes their relationship. Power tells how fast energy is converted.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

pages.title: A divider is only ideal when the load is negligible
pages.text: For two series resistors, Vout = Vin × Rbottom/(Rtop + Rbottom) when the output is unloaded. Connecting a load places that load in parallel with the bottom resistor and lowers its effective resistance, so Vout falls. A DMM usually loads the divider very little because its input resistance is high, but a sensor or following circuit may not. Thevenin thinking—source voltage plus source resistance—helps predict this behavior.
pages.remember: Before trusting a divider, ask what is connected to its output and compare impedances.
pages.sourceLesson: Series, parallel, KVL, KCL, and divider reasoning

pages.title: Atoms, charge, current, voltage, resistance, and uses of electricity
pages.text: Atoms contain positively charged protons, neutral neutrons, and negatively charged electrons. Electronics is primarily concerned with how charge carriers move or are redistributed in materials. One coulomb is a quantity of charge; one ampere is one coulomb per second. Current is therefore a rate of charge flow, while voltage is energy difference per unit charge between two points. Resistance describes how strongly a material/device opposes current for a given applied voltage. These terms are not interchangeable: a 5 V source can exist with nearly zero current when the circuit is open, and a low resistance can allow very large current if the source can supply it. Electrical energy is used for heating, light, motion, computation, communication, sensing, storage and conversion. A technician uses the same quantities whether the device is a simple resistor circuit or an embedded board: identify the source/reference, predict current paths, check voltage differences, and verify power/rating limits.
pages.sourceLesson: Series, parallel, KVL, KCL, and divider reasoning

pages.title: Resistive, capacitive, inductive and impedance behavior
pages.text: Resistors may use carbon/metal films, wirewound elements, semiconductor thermistors and other materials chosen for value range, power, stability, noise and temperature behavior. Capacitors store energy in an electric field; common constructions include ceramic, film and electrolytic devices, with polarity applying to many electrolytics. Inductors store energy in a magnetic field; turns, coil geometry, wire resistance and core material affect inductance and losses. Resistance is the real, dissipative opposition measured in ohms. Reactance is frequency-dependent opposition from capacitance or inductance: XC = 1/(2πfC) falls as frequency rises, while XL = 2πfL rises. Impedance combines resistance and reactance and therefore includes both magnitude and phase. In AC circuits, voltage/current phase relationships matter: ideal resistor V and I are in phase, ideal inductor current lags voltage, and ideal capacitor current leads voltage.
pages.sourceLesson: Series, parallel, KVL, KCL, and divider reasoning

detail.problem: A transformer has 500 primary turns and 100 secondary turns. The primary receives 120 Vrms. Estimate secondary voltage and ideal secondary current if the primary current is 50 mA.
steps: Turns ratio Np/Ns=500/100=5.
Ideal power in≈120*0.05=6 W.
Ideal Is≈6/24=0.25 A; real current will be limited by losses and ratings.
detail.answer: About 24 Vrms and 0.25 A idealized secondary current at 6 W.
detail.meaning: Turns ratio sets voltage ratio while current changes inversely in the ideal power-conservation model.

pages.title: Topology determines what is shared
pages.text: Series components carry the same current because there is only one path. Their resistances add. Parallel components share the same two nodes, so they have the same voltage; conductances add, or use 1/RT = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + …. Do not decide from how a drawing looks—identify nodes and paths. A junction can be stretched or bent on a schematic without changing the circuit.
pages.remember: Series: same current. Parallel: same voltage. Verify by nodes, not by appearance.
pages.sourceLesson: Series, parallel, KVL, KCL, and divider reasoning

pages.title: Topology comes before arithmetic
pages.text: Series and parallel are connection relationships, not visual shapes. Two components are in series only when the same current must pass through both with no branching node between them. Two branches are in parallel when both ends connect to the same pair of nodes, so they share the same voltage. Redrawing a messy schematic into clearly labeled nodes often makes the topology obvious. Only after the topology is identified should equivalent resistance formulas be used. This habit prevents one of the most common errors in electronics: applying a series or parallel formula to components that merely look adjacent on the page.
pages.sourceLesson: Series, parallel, KVL, KCL, and divider reasoning

pages.title: Kirchhoff turns conservation into two diagnostic rules
pages.text: Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law says signed voltage changes around a closed loop sum to zero. Kirchhoff’s Current Law says current entering a node equals current leaving it. These are not extra formulas competing with Ohm’s law. Ohm describes component behavior; KVL and KCL connect components into a network. If your calculated drops do not add to the source or branch currents do not recombine, the model or arithmetic is wrong.
pages.remember: Use KVL and KCL after every network calculation as built-in error detectors.
pages.sourceLesson: Series, parallel, KVL, KCL, and divider reasoning

pages.title: KCL and KVL are conservation laws
pages.text: Kirchhoff's Current Law says the algebraic sum of currents at a node is zero: charge is not disappearing at an ideal junction. Kirchhoff's Voltage Law says the algebraic sum of voltage rises and drops around a closed loop is zero: energy per unit charge is accounted for around the path. Pick a sign convention and keep it. A negative result usually means the actual direction is opposite your assumed arrow, not that the mathematics failed. These laws continue to work in circuits that cannot be reduced by simple series/parallel shortcuts.
pages.sourceLesson: Series, parallel, KVL, KCL, and divider reasoning

pages.title: A divider is only ideal when the load is negligible
pages.text: For two series resistors, Vout = Vin × Rbottom/(Rtop + Rbottom) when the output is unloaded. Connecting a load places that load in parallel with the bottom resistor and lowers its effective resistance, so Vout falls. A DMM usually loads the divider very little because its input resistance is high, but a sensor or following circuit may not. Thevenin thinking—source voltage plus source resistance—helps predict this behavior.
pages.remember: Before trusting a divider, ask what is connected to its output and compare impedances.
pages.sourceLesson: Series, parallel, KVL, KCL, and divider reasoning

pages.title: Loaded dividers reveal why measuring changes circuits
pages.text: An unloaded divider uses Vout = Vin Rbottom/(Rtop+Rbottom). Once a load is attached, the load is in parallel with the lower divider resistor, changing the effective resistance and therefore the output. This is not an edge case; it is the same mechanism behind meter loading, sensor loading, bias-network loading, and interface design. Treat every measurement device and connected stage as part of the circuit unless its impedance is large enough to ignore for the required accuracy.
pages.sourceLesson: Series, parallel, KVL, KCL, and divider reasoning

pages.title: Fault patterns have structure
pages.text: An open in a series path often creates zero current and can place nearly the full source across the break. A short across a component forces its voltage near zero and changes currents elsewhere. A wrong resistor changes proportional drops. A misplaced ground reference makes multiple good measurements look wrong. Begin by reproducing the symptom, confirming source and reference, then divide the network at a high-information node.
pages.remember: Confirm the symptom and rails before accusing a component.
pages.sourceLesson: Use expected node values to troubleshoot instead of guessing

pages.title: A schematic is a prediction map
pages.text: Mark the source, reference node, current paths, and useful test points. Calculate approximate node voltages and branch currents before connecting the meter. The expected values let each measurement answer a question: “Is power reaching this block?” “Is the divider loaded?” “Is this branch open?” Random probing produces numbers; hypothesis-driven probing produces decisions.
pages.remember: Every probe point should separate at least two plausible causes.
pages.sourceLesson: Use expected node values to troubleshoot instead of guessing

pages.title: Turn a schematic into a measurement plan
pages.text: A schematic is a map of electrical relationships, not just a drawing of parts. Start by identifying the source, ground/reference, rails, major loads, and any divider or series path. For each important node, write an expected voltage range before touching the board. If the circuit includes a divider or current-limiting resistor, calculate the expected value. If a component is polarized, note the expected polarity. This predicted-node table converts troubleshooting from 'probe until something looks strange' into a sequence of testable questions.
pages.sourceLesson: Use expected node values to troubleshoot instead of guessing

pages.title: Different faults leave different signatures
pages.text: An open resistor or broken trace often interrupts current and can create a node pulled toward another rail through remaining paths. A short can collapse a node, increase current, or force two nodes together. A wrong resistor value shifts divider voltages or bias. A wiring reversal can place the correct component on the wrong node. A heavy load can mimic a wrong resistor by changing the effective divider. Your hypothesis should therefore predict a specific measurement signature. If two hypotheses predict the same first measurement, choose another test that separates them before changing parts.
pages.sourceLesson: Use expected node values to troubleshoot instead of guessing

pages.title: Mixed practice tests selection, not just execution
pages.text: Real questions do not announce which formula to use. Before calculating, classify the circuit, identify known/unknown quantities, and choose a principle. Mix Ohm/power, series/parallel, dividers, KVL/KCL, waveform quantities, RC timing, safety, and instrument selection. This is harder than blocked practice because it trains discrimination—the exact skill needed on a broad exam and at the bench.
pages.remember: Name the principle before using it. “This is KCL because…” is part of the answer.
pages.sourceLesson: Interleaved foundation retrieval and error repair

pages.title: Use three independent checks
pages.text: Units reveal category errors, magnitude checks expose prefix mistakes, and conservation checks expose network inconsistency. Example: a 5 V source through kilohms should usually produce milliamperes, not amperes. Resistor drops in a loop should add to the source. Branch currents should recombine. Energy delivered and dissipated should make physical sense.
pages.remember: A calculator result becomes an engineering answer only after units, magnitude, and conservation agree.
pages.sourceLesson: Interleaved foundation retrieval and error repair

pages.title: Interleaving forces model selection
pages.text: Real technical work does not announce which formula or chapter applies. A mixed problem may show a wrong node voltage, a current-limited supply, and a slow waveform at the same time. The first skill is therefore classification: is the primary issue a DC network, an instrument setup, a transient, or a safety boundary? Write what quantity is unknown, what evidence is available, and which physical relationship connects them. If you reach for a formula before identifying the relationship, you are vulnerable to distractors that contain correct equations used in the wrong situation.
pages.sourceLesson: Interleaved foundation retrieval and error repair

pages.title: A correction should attack the error mechanism
pages.text: Missing a question because of unit conversion is different from missing it because KCL was misunderstood. Label misses as concept, model selection, algebra, units, diagram interpretation, instrument setup, or safety judgment. Then repair the cause. A unit miss gets prefix drills and magnitude estimation; a topology miss gets node tracing and circuit redraws; a safety miss gets a stop/verify rehearsal. Re-reading the whole chapter is often less effective than a short, changed problem that directly targets the error.
pages.sourceLesson: Interleaved foundation retrieval and error repair

examples.title: Series, parallel, KVL, KCL, and divider reasoning

detail.problem: A 12 V source feeds 2 kΩ in series with 4 kΩ. Find current, both drops, and unloaded output across 4 kΩ.
steps: RT = 2 kΩ + 4 kΩ = 6 kΩ.
I = 12 V / 6 kΩ = 2 mA.
V2k = 2 mA × 2 kΩ = 4 V.
V4k = 2 mA × 4 kΩ = 8 V.
KVL check: 4 V + 8 V = 12 V.
detail.answer: 2 mA, 4 V, and 8 V.
detail.transfer: If a 4 kΩ load is attached across the lower 4 kΩ, the lower equivalent becomes 2 kΩ; the output becomes 6 V, not 8 V.

examples.title: Series, parallel, KVL, KCL, and divider reasoning

detail.problem: A 12 V divider uses 3.3 kOhm on top and 2.2 kOhm on bottom. Find unloaded Vout, then find Vout when a 2.2 kOhm load is connected from output to ground.
steps: Loaded lower leg: 2.2 kOhm || 2.2 kOhm = 1.1 kOhm.
The heavy load changes the circuit substantially; the original divider equation using 2.2 kOhm alone is no longer valid.
detail.answer: 4.8 V unloaded and 3.0 V with the 2.2 kOhm load.
detail.meaning: A connected instrument or downstream stage can become part of the network and change the value being measured.

examples.title: Use expected node values to troubleshoot instead of guessing

detail.problem: A 10 V divider uses equal 10 kΩ resistors, but Vout measures 0 V. The top node is 10 V and the midpoint-to-ground resistance is nearly 0 Ω with power off.
steps: Expected unloaded Vout is 5 V.
A confirmed 10 V top node rules out the source path.
Near-zero midpoint-to-ground resistance is inconsistent with the intended 10 kΩ lower leg.
Inspect for a solder bridge or wiring short from midpoint to ground before replacing both resistors.
detail.answer: The evidence points to a midpoint-to-ground short.
detail.transfer: This is divide-and-conquer: one high-information node and one power-off check separate a rail problem from a network short.

examples.title: Use expected node values to troubleshoot instead of guessing

detail.problem: A 12 V divider should produce 4 V from 2 kOhm over 1 kOhm. You measure 12 V at the input, 0 V at the output, and the lower resistor measures 1 kOhm power-off.
steps: Expected current is 12/(2k+1k)=4 mA and Vout=4 V.
0 V at the output is consistent with the node being shorted to ground, the upper resistor being open, or the source path to the upper resistor being broken.
Because the lower resistor is confirmed near 1 kOhm, measure voltage on both sides of the upper resistor under safe power.
If the source side is 12 V and output side 0 V, power down and test the upper resistor/trace for an open; if both sides are 0 V, move upstream toward the source connection.
detail.answer: Use one measurement at the upper-resistor boundary to separate an upstream supply-path fault from an open upper leg or grounded output.
detail.meaning: The next test is chosen because its possible outcomes separate competing causes.

examples.title: Interleaved foundation retrieval and error repair

detail.problem: A student calculates 5 V / 2 kΩ = 2.5 A and a two-resistor loop whose drops total 8 V on a 6 V source.
steps: Unit check: V/kΩ yields mA, so the first answer should be 2.5 mA.
Magnitude check: kilohms at a few volts cannot draw amperes.
KVL check: 8 V of passive drops cannot be supported by a single 6 V source in the stated loop.
Redo both problems and identify whether the fault is prefix conversion, sign, or topology.
detail.answer: Both answers fail independent checks before any bench work begins.
detail.transfer: The same checks prevent unsafe supply settings and speed fault isolation.

pages.title: Each drawing answers a different question
pages.text: A block diagram shows functions and flow; a schematic shows electrical connectivity and component relationships; a wiring diagram emphasizes physical interconnection; a layout/PCB view shows physical placement/traces; a timing diagram shows logic versus time. Do not demand pin routing from a block diagram or infer physical proximity from a schematic. Cross-reference designators and connector pin numbers across artifacts.
pages.remember: Name the question first, then choose the artifact that can answer it.
pages.sourceLesson: Read diagram types and turn symbols into behavior

pages.title: Symbols, schematic/wiring/block diagrams, drafting conventions, and IC pinouts
pages.text: A schematic shows electrical function and connectivity rather than physical placement; a wiring diagram emphasizes actual terminals, wire paths or harness connections; a block diagram suppresses detail to show functional stages and signal/energy flow. Symbols communicate device type and terminal relationships, but the exact component value, reference designator and pin numbers still matter. Drafting conventions such as reference designators, net labels, junction dots, connector pin numbers, power/ground symbols, sheet references and consistent signal direction reduce ambiguity. Crossing lines are not automatically connected—look for the drawing convention/junction indication. ICs require exact package and datasheet pinout: pin 1/orientation, VCC/VDD, ground/reference, inputs, outputs, enable/reset and special pins can vary even when package shapes look similar. Never transfer a pinout from a “similar looking” IC without verifying the exact part/revision.
pages.sourceLesson: Read diagram types and turn symbols into behavior

pages.title: Block diagrams, test points, signal tracing, and schematic fault location
pages.text: Troubleshooting begins by turning the product into functional stages: source/power, input conditioning, processing, drivers and output are common examples. A block diagram helps choose boundaries; the schematic provides component-level paths. Test points are deliberately accessible nodes chosen because their expected voltage, waveform, logic state or signal can prove whether a stage is operating. Signal tracing applies a known input, predicts what should appear at successive points, and finds the first boundary where expected behavior disappears or changes incorrectly. Tracing can proceed input-to-output, output-to-input or by half-split depending on access and risk. The goal is not to measure every point; it is to choose a point whose possible outcomes separate hypotheses. Always preserve common reference/ground and loading limits. Once the first bad boundary is located, the schematic narrows the suspect components/connections between the last-good and first-bad nodes.
pages.sourceLesson: Read diagram types and turn symbols into behavior

pages.title: Schematic, wiring, block, and layout drawings have different purposes
pages.text: A schematic shows electrical relationships and functional connectivity, not physical placement. A wiring diagram emphasizes terminals, harnesses, connectors, and point-to-point connections. A block diagram abstracts groups of circuitry into functions and signal flow. PCB/layout or assembly drawings show physical arrangement. Mixing these interpretations causes mistakes: two schematic wires may cross without connecting, and components drawn far apart can share the same net. Read the legend, reference designators, net labels, connector pin numbers, and active-low notation before tracing behavior.
pages.sourceLesson: Read diagram types and turn symbols into behavior

pages.title: The DMM is several instruments sharing one display
pages.text: DC volts measures average potential difference with polarity; AC volts reports an AC magnitude whose accuracy depends on bandwidth and RMS method. Resistance/continuity uses an internal source and requires a de-energized circuit. Diode mode applies a small current and reports forward voltage. Current mode routes circuit current through a shunt and a fuse. Autorange chooses scale, but it cannot choose the correct mode, jack, or placement for you.
pages.remember: A display value is trustworthy only when mode, jack, range, connection, and instrument limits are known.
pages.sourceLesson: What each instrument measures and how the controls map to quantities

pages.title: Analog/digital meters, construction, safety, loading, and leads
pages.text: An analog meter movement responds to current and uses resistors/shunts/rectification to create ranges; a digital multimeter converts an input through protection/ranging and an ADC to a numeric display. Voltage mode presents high input impedance and is connected in parallel. Current mode routes current through a low-value shunt/fuse and is inserted in series; placing a current-configured meter across a source can create a dangerous short. Resistance/continuity applies an internal test source and belongs on a de-energized circuit. Meter loading occurs because the instrument is not infinite impedance: a low input resistance can pull a high-impedance node away from its normal voltage. Safety means correct category/voltage/current rating, intact case/leads/fuses, correct jack and mode, and staying within the task’s permitted energy level. Test leads are equipment: inspect insulation, finger guards, shrouds and tips, and replace damaged leads rather than taping over unsafe damage.
pages.sourceLesson: What each instrument measures and how the controls map to quantities

pages.title: Reproducibility belongs in the measurement
pages.text: Record circuit revision, power settings and current limit, instrument model when relevant, probe attenuation, coupling, bandwidth limit, vertical scale, timebase, trigger, test point, reference, and observed value. Include a screenshot only after those facts are known. State tolerance or uncertainty honestly: component tolerance, meter accuracy, probe loading, noise, and reading resolution can explain small deviations.
pages.remember: A screenshot without setup and expected behavior is decoration, not engineering evidence.
pages.sourceLesson: Measurement planning, probe discipline, and uncertainty

pages.title: Write the question before choosing the probe
pages.text: A professional measurement begins with a decision question such as 'Is the 3.3 V rail collapsing during radio transmit?' or 'Does the MCU pin actually toggle after the register is set?' From that question, define the quantity, expected range, reference, instrument, connection, bandwidth/time resolution, and stop condition. Without the question, it is easy to collect screenshots that look technical but do not distinguish any cause. A good plan predicts what each hypothesis would produce before measurement, which turns the instrument into a reasoning tool rather than a camera.
pages.sourceLesson: Measurement planning, probe discipline, and uncertainty

pages.title: Technician application: schematics, datasheets, design intent, and test-point prediction
pages.text: Professional schematic reading is prediction before probing. Start at power/ground and connectors, follow reference designators and signal direction, identify functional blocks, then use the exact component datasheet to confirm pinout, absolute maximum ratings, recommended operating conditions and electrical characteristics. Absolute maximum is a damage boundary, not a normal design target. Choose the drawing type for the question: schematic for electrical function, wiring/harness for physical connection, block diagram for stages, PCB/layout for physical location/routing, timing diagram for time relationships. Support parts such as pull-ups/pull-downs, decoupling capacitors, series/current-limiting resistors and clamps often reveal design intent. Mark expected node voltages/waveforms and useful test points before touching an instrument; those predictions become the troubleshooting acceptance criteria.
pages.sourceLesson: Troubleshoot with competing hypotheses and high-information tests

pages.title: Building wiring awareness and flowcharts
pages.text: Electronics technicians often interface equipment with building power, grounding, branch circuits, receptacles, low-voltage pathways and communications cabling. They need enough premises-wiring awareness to recognize source voltage, grounding/bonding context, breaker/branch identity, receptacle condition, separation requirements and when work belongs to a qualified electrician. This course does not authorize mains installation or energized premises work. Flowcharts are different from schematics: they represent decisions, sequence and process state using start/end, action and decision branches. A flowchart can describe a troubleshooting procedure, boot sequence or test algorithm even when no electrical connection is shown. Use a schematic to understand where current/signal can travel and a flowchart to understand what action or decision happens next.
pages.sourceLesson: Read diagram types and turn symbols into behavior

pages.title: Symbols become useful when connected to expected behavior
pages.text: Recognizing a symbol is only the first step. For a resistor divider, predict node voltage; for a diode, identify polarity and expected conduction direction; for a transistor, identify control terminal and current path; for an op-amp, identify feedback sign; for an IC, use the exact pinout rather than assuming a package pin from memory. Test points are chosen at meaningful boundaries where a voltage, waveform, or logic state can prove whether a stage works. A schematic supports troubleshooting when each node is converted into an expected observation.
pages.sourceLesson: Read diagram types and turn symbols into behavior

pages.title: Signal tracing uses hierarchy
pages.text: Start with a block diagram or functional path to avoid drowning in components. Choose a midpoint or stage boundary, then use the schematic to identify exact nodes and parts. Apply a known input and trace forward, backward from the output, or use half-split/divide-and-conquer. The last known-good and first bad boundary localize the fault region. Flowcharts serve the same purpose for procedural or software behavior: they show decisions, states, and sequence that can be compared with observed execution.
pages.sourceLesson: Read diagram types and turn symbols into behavior

examples.title: What each instrument measures and how the controls map to quantities

detail.problem: A waveform spans 4 vertical divisions at 0.5 V/div and one cycle spans 5 horizontal divisions at 200 µs/div.
steps: Vpp = 4 × 0.5 V = 2.0 V peak-to-peak.
Confirm the probe/channel attenuation setting before accepting amplitude.
detail.answer: 2.0 Vpp and 1 kHz.
detail.transfer: If the 10× probe is set to 10× but the channel assumes 1×, the amplitude display will be wrong even though the trace looks stable.

examples.title: What each instrument measures and how the controls map to quantities

detail.problem: A 3.3 V digital output appears as 0.33 V on the oscilloscope, while a DMM reads 3.29 V.
steps: The DMM suggests the node's DC level is near 3.3 V.
A factor-of-ten scope discrepancy strongly suggests probe attenuation mismatch: for example a 10x probe with the channel set to 1x, or vice versa.
Verify probe switch position and channel probe factor before changing the circuit.
Also verify the ground/reference point and DC coupling.
detail.answer: Check probe attenuation/configuration and reference before concluding the digital output is only 0.33 V.
detail.meaning: Instrument configuration is part of the measurement and can create a false fault symptom.

examples.title: Measurement planning, probe discipline, and uncertainty

detail.problem: A 100 mV ripple rides on a 5 V rail. The scope trace is off-screen at a sensitive vertical scale.
steps: Keep the ground clip on the approved circuit reference.
Start in DC coupling to confirm the 5 V level and safe signal range.
Use vertical position/offset or then AC coupling to examine the small ripple.
Enable an appropriate bandwidth limit if high-frequency noise is not the question.
Record that AC coupling removed the DC component; do not report the trace as absolute rail voltage.
detail.answer: Verify the DC level first, then isolate ripple with documented coupling and scale.
detail.transfer: This same sequence is used to characterize regulator ripple without losing the fact that a DC rail is present.

examples.title: Measurement planning, probe discipline, and uncertainty

detail.problem: A UART line should idle at 3.3 V and transmit bursts every second. A scope capture shows 2.1 V average with no obvious transitions.
steps: The word 'average' suggests the measurement may not be configured to reveal digital timing.
Verify the probe reference, attenuation, DC coupling, and vertical scale.
Set a time base that can show the 1 s burst interval or use single/normal trigger on an edge; then zoom into the bit timing.
If the line still sits near 2.1 V, investigate contention, wrong voltage domain, heavy loading, or incorrect pull network.
detail.answer: First prove the measurement setup can reveal the expected idle level and transitions, then treat a persistent 2.1 V level as an electrical fault symptom.
detail.meaning: A measurement plan separates 'the signal is wrong' from 'the observation method cannot show the signal.'

Identify Duty Cycle and Pulse Width DC sources

pages.title: A waveform needs both vertical and horizontal descriptions
pages.text: Amplitude may mean peak from the center/reference, peak-to-peak between extremes, or RMS as an equivalent heating value. For a zero-offset sine wave, Vrms = Vpk/√2 and Vpp = 2Vpk; do not apply that RMS shortcut to arbitrary shapes. Frequency is cycles per second and period is seconds per cycle: f = 1/T. Phase compares timing between equal-frequency waveforms. DC offset shifts the entire waveform above or below zero.
pages.remember: Always attach the qualifier: Vpk, Vpp, Vrms, frequency, phase, and offset are different facts.
pages.sourceLesson: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

pages.title: Waveform vocabulary connects the time domain to measurements
pages.text: Amplitude must be named precisely: peak, peak-to-peak, RMS, average, offset, duty cycle, pulse width, rise/fall time, and period answer different questions. For a sine wave, Vrms = Vpk/sqrt(2); for arbitrary waveforms the relationship differs. Frequency is 1/period. A pulse train can have a 10% duty cycle even if its repetition frequency is low. Reading the waveform correctly is a prerequisite for later filter, timing, power, and digital-interface analysis.
pages.sourceLesson: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

pages.title: The DMM is several instruments sharing one display
pages.text: DC volts measures average potential difference with polarity; AC volts reports an AC magnitude whose accuracy depends on bandwidth and RMS method. Resistance/continuity uses an internal source and requires a de-energized circuit. Diode mode applies a small current and reports forward voltage. Current mode routes circuit current through a shunt and a fuse. Autorange chooses scale, but it cannot choose the correct mode, jack, or placement for you.
pages.remember: A display value is trustworthy only when mode, jack, range, connection, and instrument limits are known.
pages.sourceLesson: What each instrument measures and how the controls map to quantities

pages.title: An oscilloscope is a voltage-versus-time instrument
pages.text: Vertical scale sets volts per division; horizontal scale sets seconds per division. Probe attenuation must match the channel setting or displayed amplitude is wrong by a factor such as ten. Trigger level and slope choose a repeatable point in the waveform so it appears stable. DC coupling preserves offset; AC coupling blocks the DC component for viewing small variation. Period is horizontal divisions × time/div, and frequency is 1/period.
pages.remember: Before measuring, state expected amplitude, offset, frequency, and reference location.
pages.sourceLesson: What each instrument measures and how the controls map to quantities

pages.title: Oscilloscope controls and spectrum analyzer operation
pages.text: An oscilloscope displays voltage versus time. Vertical scale controls volts/division; vertical position establishes where the trace sits; coupling selects DC, AC or ground/reference behavior; probe factor must match the probe; horizontal time/division controls the visible time span; trigger source/level/slope/event stabilizes acquisition relative to a repeatable point; bandwidth/sample-rate/acquisition settings affect what can be trusted. Measure amplitude only after confirming probe factor and reference, and distinguish peak, peak-to-peak and RMS. A spectrum analyzer displays amplitude/power versus frequency. Center frequency and span choose the region, reference level and input attenuation protect/scale the input, and resolution bandwidth (RBW) trades frequency resolution against sweep/noise behavior; video bandwidth (VBW) smooths displayed noise. A spectrum analyzer answers “what frequencies are present,” while a scope answers “how does voltage change with time.” Neither input should be exposed to an unknown signal beyond its rated level.
pages.sourceLesson: What each instrument measures and how the controls map to quantities

pages.title: Signal generators, frequency counters, RCL substitution, and ESR meters
pages.text: A signal generator supplies a controlled test stimulus such as sine, square, pulse, sweep, audio/RF or function-generator output. Set waveform, amplitude, offset, frequency, source impedance and load assumptions before connection. A frequency counter measures event rate by counting cycles over a gate/timebase or related technique; accuracy is limited by timebase quality, gate time, trigger/signal level, noise and bandwidth. R-C-L substitution boxes provide known selectable resistance, capacitance or inductance so a technician can test whether circuit behavior changes when a suspected value is replaced under safe conditions; they are not a substitute for understanding voltage/current/power ratings. ESR meters estimate equivalent series resistance, particularly useful for finding degraded electrolytic capacitors whose capacitance may look plausible while internal loss is high. In-circuit readings can be influenced by parallel paths, so the measurement method and circuit state matter.
pages.sourceLesson: What each instrument measures and how the controls map to quantities

pages.title: Logic probes and logic pulsers: observe versus stimulate
pages.text: A logic probe is an observing instrument for digital nodes. Referenced to circuit ground and operated within its supported logic-family/voltage range, it indicates logic HIGH, LOW, and on many probes pulsing/activity. It does not tell you that a HIGH is “good” unless the expected logic state and threshold family are known. A logic pulser is the complementary stimulus tool: it injects a brief controlled logic transition or pulse at a node so the technician can see whether downstream logic responds. Used with a logic probe, oscilloscope or logic analyzer, it can separate “the upstream stage never changes” from “the downstream stage cannot respond.” Before pulsing, verify circuit supply/logic family, node direction, drive capability and that forcing the node will not create destructive bus contention or violate an analog/sensitive node. Example: if an AND-gate output is stuck, verify its supply and static inputs, safely pulse one eligible input while the other is at the enabling state, and observe the output. If the input changes but the output never follows, the gate/output path becomes a stronger suspect.
pages.sourceLesson: What each instrument measures and how the controls map to quantities

pages.title: Oscilloscopes measure voltage over time
pages.text: A scope's vertical system sets volts per division, coupling, position, and probe factor; the horizontal system sets time per division and acquisition span; the trigger tells the scope where in a repeating event to align acquisitions. A waveform that looks unstable may simply be poorly triggered. A waveform that looks too small may have a 10x probe-factor mismatch. AC coupling removes DC content from the displayed path, which can hide offset information. Bandwidth and sample rate limit which details can be trusted. Always record reference point, probe attenuation, coupling, vertical scale, time base, and trigger conditions with a capture.
pages.sourceLesson: What each instrument measures and how the controls map to quantities

pages.title: Instrument choice follows the question
pages.text: A DMM is excellent for stable DC quantities and many low-frequency checks; a scope reveals time-varying amplitude, timing, ringing, glitches, and transients; a frequency counter can measure periodic frequency precisely under suitable signal conditions; a signal generator creates a known stimulus; a spectrum analyzer shows magnitude versus frequency; ESR and substitution tools answer component-specific troubleshooting questions. The correct instrument is the one that can observe the behavior that would distinguish your hypotheses without violating circuit or instrument limits.
pages.sourceLesson: What each instrument measures and how the controls map to quantities

pages.title: Measure response as a ratio across frequency
pages.text: Keep input amplitude controlled, choose several frequencies below, near, and above predicted cutoff, and record Vout/Vin. One screenshot proves one condition; a table reveals the response. Check generator source impedance and probe loading when results differ. A wrong probe factor can make both signals appear inconsistent, while a loose ground produces noise and ringing.
pages.remember: Change frequency deliberately and keep other variables fixed.
pages.sourceLesson: Turn time-domain measurements into filter and fault evidence

pages.title: Core formulas, SI prefixes, NIST spelling exceptions, and scientific notation
pages.text: Technician math begins by writing the relationship with units. Core relationships include V=IR, P=VI, f=1/T, wavelength λ=v/f, XC=1/(2πfC), XL=2πfL and resonant frequency f0=1/(2π√LC), along with context-specific ratios such as transformer turns and dB. SI prefixes are powers of ten: p 10⁻¹², n 10⁻⁹, µ 10⁻⁶, m 10⁻³, k 10³, M 10⁶, G 10⁹. Prefix case matters: m is milli while M is mega. Scientific notation keeps the coefficient times 10^n and makes prefix conversion visible. NIST writing guidance includes traditional unit-name spellings such as kilohm and megohm as exceptions to simply joining a prefix name to “ohm”; symbols remain kΩ and MΩ. Correct calculations keep units through substitution and make an order-of-magnitude estimate before trusting a calculator.
pages.sourceLesson: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

pages.title: A filter is a transfer relationship, not a label
pages.text: Calling a circuit 'low-pass' is only the start. A useful characterization states input waveform and amplitude, source impedance, output node, load, component values, frequency, and measured gain/phase or time response. In a simple RC low-pass, the output across the capacitor is near the input at frequencies far below cutoff and attenuates as frequency increases. In a high-pass, the output location is changed so low-frequency content is attenuated. The cutoff of a first-order RC network is fc = 1/(2 pi RC), but real source/load impedances modify the effective R and therefore the observed response.
pages.sourceLesson: Turn time-domain measurements into filter and fault evidence

pages.title: Time-domain and frequency-domain evidence describe the same network
pages.text: A square wave contains a fundamental plus harmonics. A low-pass filter that removes higher harmonics rounds the edges; a high-pass emphasizes transitions and may produce pulses or droop depending on time constant. A step response reveals settling and time constant; a sine sweep reveals gain versus frequency. If the time waveform and frequency response disagree with the model, check probe loading, generator source impedance, component tolerance, output node, and whether the chosen frequency actually brackets the cutoff.
pages.sourceLesson: Turn time-domain measurements into filter and fault evidence

pages.title: Decibels and graphs as engineering representations
pages.text: Decibels express ratios logarithmically. For power ratios use 10 log10(P2/P1); for voltage ratios use 20 log10(V2/V1) only when the impedances are equal or the context justifies that conversion. +3 dB is about twice power, -3 dB about half power, +10 dB ten times power, and -10 dB one tenth. Absolute levels such as dBm add a reference; 0 dBm is 1 mW. Graphs reveal relationships that a single number hides: waveform plots show value versus time, frequency-response plots show gain/phase versus frequency, IV curves show device behavior, and trend plots show drift/repeatability. Always label axes, units, scale type (linear/log), reference and conditions; otherwise a graph can be technically true but misleading.
pages.sourceLesson: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

detail.problem: A 10 kΩ resistor charges a 10 µF capacitor from a 5 V step. Find τ and approximate voltage after one τ.
steps: After one τ, the capacitor has completed about 63% of the change.
After about 5τ = 0.5 s, it is near the final value.
detail.answer: τ = 0.1 s; Vc at one τ is about 3.15 V.
detail.transfer: A scope cursor can test both the predicted time and voltage on the charging curve.

examples.title: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

detail.problem: A 10 kOhm resistor charges a 100 uF capacitor from 0 V toward 5 V. Find tau and estimate voltage after one tau and five tau.
steps: After one tau, Vc≈0.632 x 5 V = 3.16 V.
After five tau, the capacitor is above 99% of the way to 5 V, roughly 4.97 V.
The current is initially 5/10k=0.5 mA and decreases as Vc rises.
detail.answer: tau=1 s; about 3.16 V at 1 s and approximately 5 V by 5 s.
detail.meaning: The time constant predicts the shape and timing of a real charging waveform.
