objectives.title: Explain shock hazards when servicing power supplies in electronic equipment
Describe the differences between transformer powered supplies and line-connected supplies
Describe battery supplies and list common usages:
Explain battery recharging principles
Explain the reasons for filtering, describe hum, and identify common filter types:
“L” (L-section, choke or inductor) filter – an inductor in series with a capacitor in parallel
“T” filter –add a second choke on output side, taking the output across the capacitor
“Pi” filter – a single inductor with a capacitor at each end to common
Explain the reasons for power supply regulation and list common components used in regulated supplies
Explain the term ‘Integrated high voltage transformer’ supply and explain how it differs from direct or other power supply types
Explain how multiple output supplies can supply more than one voltage

Explain where fuses and circuit breakers are commonly and electrically located in circuits; approximate fuse sizes for common circuits; common fuses and circuit breaker configuration and precautions for replacement in a house service box
Explain how to calculate DC voltages from power supply circuits
Identify and analyze rectifier circuits
Describe switch mode power supply operation

pages.title: The filter capacitor supplies load between peaks
pages.text: After the rectified waveform charges the capacitor near a peak, the load discharges it until the next charging interval. A useful first estimate is ΔV ≈ Iload/(fripple C). More load current, lower ripple frequency, or smaller capacitance increases ripple. Diode drops, transformer regulation, ESR, and conduction angle alter real results. Capacitor voltage and polarity require margin.
pages.remember: Ripple is charge removed divided by capacitance; write the ripple frequency explicitly.
pages.sourceLesson: Power-supply blocks and their expected signals

pages.title: Rectification, L/T/Pi filters, regulation, and DC calculations
pages.text: Rectifiers convert AC into unidirectional pulsating voltage. A half-wave circuit uses one polarity; a full-wave center-tapped or bridge rectifier uses both halves, increasing ripple frequency. A reservoir capacitor charges near waveform peaks and supplies load current between peaks, reducing hum/ripple. L-section filtering uses a series choke/inductor followed by a shunt capacitor; a T filter adds a second series choke after the capacitor; a Pi filter uses capacitor–inductor–capacitor so its schematic resembles π. These filters trade ripple reduction against size, loss, inrush and dynamic response. Regulation keeps output near target despite input/load changes using Zener, linear regulator, feedback/pass devices or switching methods. Multiple-output supplies can use separate windings/regulators or derived rails, each with its own current and reference limits. For sine-fed rectifiers, begin from the correct RMS-to-peak relationship (Vpk≈Vrms√2), then subtract appropriate diode drops and account for load/ripple rather than assuming the capacitor always sits at unloaded peak.
pages.sourceLesson: Power-supply blocks and their expected signals

pages.title: Use rail behavior to distinguish source, regulator, and load faults
pages.text: If a regulator input is correct but output is low, possibilities include overload/short, regulator shutdown/current limit, insufficient headroom, bad enable, thermal protection, wrong feedback, or failed part. If both input and output collapse under load, move upstream. If output is correct unloaded but collapses with a downstream connector, isolate that load. Measure current and temperature where appropriate. A rail that looks correct on a DMM may still contain reset-causing dips or ripple, so use the scope when timing matters.
pages.sourceLesson: Rail-by-rail bring-up and supply troubleshooting

pages.title: A diode is directional but not an ideal check valve
pages.text: A forward-biased junction conducts with a device- and current-dependent voltage; a silicon rectifier may be near 0.6–0.8 V in common conditions, while LEDs vary strongly by color and current. Reverse bias normally blocks until leakage or breakdown. Rectifier diodes steer power, Zeners operate in controlled breakdown for reference/clamping, LEDs emit light, and protection diodes redirect transients. Always check current, reverse voltage, power, and speed.
pages.remember: Direction is only the first question; operating current, voltage, dissipation, and transient behavior complete it.
pages.sourceLesson: Junction behavior and semiconductor device roles

pages.title: A MOSFET is controlled by gate-to-source voltage
pages.text: An enhancement-mode N-channel MOSFET conducts when VGS is high enough, but VGS(th) only marks the beginning of conduction at a small current. Low RDS(on) must be specified at the actual gate drive. The insulated gate draws little DC current but has capacitance and is ESD-sensitive. Body diode, voltage rating, current, power, switching speed, and gate protection all matter. SCRs/TRIACs are latching/AC-control devices with different turn-off behavior.
pages.remember: Always reason with VGS relative to source—not gate voltage relative to an unrelated ground.
pages.sourceLesson: Junction behavior and semiconductor device roles

pages.title: Follow the block chain
pages.text: A conventional supply changes/isolate voltage when needed, rectifies AC to one polarity, stores energy in a filter capacitor, regulates output, and protects against abnormal current/voltage/temperature. Half-wave uses one portion of the cycle; full-wave/bridge uses both and produces ripple at twice line frequency. In this course, mains-side construction or probing is prohibited; use isolated low-voltage AC/simulation or ready-made safe supplies.
pages.remember: Input conversion → rectification → filtering → regulation → protection → load.
pages.sourceLesson: Power-supply blocks and their expected signals

pages.title: Power problems are upstream until evidence says otherwise
pages.text: Begin with a block diagram and expected value at each boundary. Confirm source, then rectified node, filtered node, regulator input/output, and load. A missing upstream node invalidates downstream conclusions. A rail that is correct unloaded but collapses under load points to current limit, source impedance, regulator dropout/thermal limit, wiring, or load fault.
pages.remember: Measure in causal order and compare every node with a stated expectation.
pages.sourceLesson: Rail-by-rail bring-up and supply troubleshooting

pages.title: Regulation trades voltage, current, heat, noise, and complexity
pages.text: A linear regulator dissipates roughly (Vin − Vout)Iload and is simple/quiet but may need dropout headroom and thermal management. A switching regulator stores/transfers energy with inductors/capacitors for higher efficiency but adds switching ripple, layout, and control complexity. Line regulation describes output change versus input; load regulation versus load; efficiency is Pout/Pin.
pages.remember: A correct output voltage does not prove acceptable ripple, thermal margin, efficiency, or load behavior.
pages.sourceLesson: Power-supply blocks and their expected signals

pages.title: Ripple measurement can be corrupted by the probe loop
pages.text: Confirm the DC rail with a DMM/scope in DC coupling, then use a short ground connection, appropriate bandwidth limit, and AC coupling or offset to examine small ripple. A long ground lead can pick up switching fields and show ringing that is mostly measurement loop. Record both time-domain settings and load condition.
pages.remember: Small-signal rail measurements demand a physically small probe loop and explicit bandwidth.
pages.sourceLesson: Rail-by-rail bring-up and supply troubleshooting

pages.title: Power-supply hazards, transformer versus line-connected supplies, and protection
pages.text: Power supplies can contain hazardous mains voltage and stored capacitor energy even after the output appears low-voltage. A traditional transformer-isolated supply has galvanic separation between primary and secondary, but primary circuitry remains hazardous and the secondary may still store significant energy. Line-connected/non-isolated supplies reference parts of the circuitry directly to mains and require isolation-rated service methods. An integrated high-voltage transformer (IHVT, historically common in CRT/display high-voltage sections and often implemented as a flyback-style transformer assembly) combines the high-voltage transformer with associated rectification/multiplier or output functions in a compact module. It develops kilovolt-level output from switched/pulsed energy rather than simply passing line-frequency mains through an ordinary power transformer, and it can retain hazardous charge after power is removed. Treat the exact discharge, replacement, and servicing instructions for the product as authoritative. Overcurrent protection is normally placed so a fault is interrupted near the source before conductors/components overheat. Fuses/breakers are selected from equipment documentation and circuit requirements; house-service replacement is outside this course unless the person is qualified/authorized. Never “approximate” an unknown fuse upward. A replacement must match type, voltage, current and interrupting rating, and the underlying fault must be investigated.
pages.sourceLesson: Power-supply blocks and their expected signals

pages.title: Start with a power tree
pages.text: Before probing, draw or read the power tree: connector/source, input protection, pre-regulator or converter, individual rails, enable signals, loads, reset/brownout connections, and test points. For each rail, record nominal voltage, tolerance, expected current, sequencing or startup timing, and what subsystem it powers. This prevents the common mistake of finding one good 3.3 V test point and assuming every power domain is healthy. Modern boards often have separate core, analog, I/O, sensor, and radio rails.
pages.sourceLesson: Rail-by-rail bring-up and supply troubleshooting

pages.title: Document staged bring-up
pages.text: Apply power with a defined current limit, observe startup current, verify the first rail, then enable or connect later domains one at a time if the design allows. Stop at the first unexpected current, voltage, temperature, smell, or waveform. Save a known-good table of rail voltages/current and startup behavior. That baseline becomes a reference for later faults and prevents repeated rediscovery of normal measurements.
pages.sourceLesson: Rail-by-rail bring-up and supply troubleshooting

pages.title: Switch-mode power supply operation
pages.text: A switch-mode power supply regulates energy by rapidly switching a semiconductor rather than continuously dissipating the full voltage difference in a pass device. The switch, inductor/transformer or other energy-storage element, diode or synchronous switch, output capacitor and feedback controller form a power-conversion loop. In a buck converter, the switching node alternates between source and ground-side states; the inductor/capacitor average that pulsed energy to a lower DC output. A boost converter rearranges energy transfer so output can exceed input. Flyback supplies store energy in a coupled magnetic element and can provide isolation. The controller changes duty cycle, frequency or pulse pattern according to feedback and protection limits. Technician symptoms include no switching, shorted switch, startup cycling, excessive ripple, wrong duty cycle, feedback/reference fault, overloaded/shorted output, dried capacitors and EMI/noise problems. Oscilloscope probing of primary-side switching nodes can be hazardous; use only rated/isolation procedures within training.
pages.sourceLesson: Power-supply blocks and their expected signals

pages.title: Linear supplies move through recognizable blocks
pages.text: A traditional isolated linear supply may use transformer -> rectifier -> reservoir filter -> regulator -> load. The transformer changes AC voltage and can provide isolation. The rectifier converts alternating polarity into pulsating DC. The reservoir capacitor stores energy between peaks, reducing ripple. The regulator holds the output near a target despite input/load variation within its operating limits. Each block has an expected waveform: sine before rectification, full-wave pulses after a bridge, rippled DC at the reservoir, and lower-ripple regulated DC at the output. Troubleshooting becomes much easier when those waveforms are predicted before probing.
pages.sourceLesson: Power-supply blocks and their expected signals

examples.title: Power-supply blocks and their expected signals

detail.problem: A full-wave 100 Hz ripple supply provides 50 mA to a 1,000 µF capacitor. Estimate peak-to-peak ripple.
steps: ΔV ≈ 0.50 V peak-to-peak.
Treat this as a first estimate; diode conduction and ESR affect the measured waveform.
detail.answer: About 0.5 Vpp ripple.
detail.transfer: Doubling capacitance or ripple frequency halves the first-order ripple estimate.

examples.title: Power-supply blocks and their expected signals

detail.problem: A full-wave rectified 60 Hz supply uses 2200 uF and draws 0.20 A. Estimate capacitor ripple using deltaV≈I/(fC).
steps: Full-wave ripple frequency is approximately 120 Hz.
deltaV≈0.20/(120*0.0022)=0.758 V peak-to-peak approximate ripple.
The estimate ignores diode conduction angle, ESR, transformer regulation, and regulator behavior but gives useful scale.
detail.answer: Approximately 0.76 Vpp ripple at the reservoir capacitor in the simplified model.
detail.meaning: Ripple is a predictable function of load, capacitance, and recharge frequency, so a measured excess can guide diagnosis.

examples.title: Rail-by-rail bring-up and supply troubleshooting

detail.problem: A 3.3 V rail is correct with no load, drops to 2.4 V at 100 mA, and the bench supply remains in CV mode.
steps: The bench source is not current limiting.
Measure regulator input under load to check dropout/source path.
If input remains adequate, check regulator rating, thermal state, wiring resistance, and load current.
If input also falls, move upstream to source/rectifier/filter connections.
detail.answer: Use input-under-load to separate upstream collapse from regulator/load behavior.
detail.transfer: A two-node comparison provides more information than swapping the regulator immediately.

examples.title: Rail-by-rail bring-up and supply troubleshooting

detail.problem: A board has 12 V input, 5 V buck output, and 3.3 V LDO from the 5 V rail. Measurements: 12.1 V input, 5.0 V, 0.8 V at 3.3 V rail, LDO hot.
steps: The 12 V source and 5 V converter are likely functioning under this condition.
The 3.3 V LDO has adequate 5 V input but is hot with low output, suggesting overload/short, wrong orientation/part, or regulator fault/current limit.
Power down and measure 3.3 V rail resistance/inspect downstream loads before replacing the LDO.
If isolating a connector restores normal 3.3 V, move diagnosis into the disconnected load branch.
detail.answer: Focus on the 3.3 V regulator/load domain; the evidence does not support replacing the upstream 12-to-5 V converter.
detail.meaning: A power tree lets one measurement localize the failing domain.

examples.title: Junction behavior and semiconductor device roles

detail.problem: A 5 V supply drives a red LED approximated at 1.9 V with a 330 Ω resistor. Estimate current and resistor power.
steps: Resistor voltage = 5 − 1.9 = 3.1 V.
P resistor = I²R ≈ 0.029 W.
Verify the actual LED datasheet and current target; forward voltage is not exact.
detail.answer: About 9.4 mA and 29 mW in the resistor.
detail.transfer: This same load current becomes the minimum current the transistor switch must handle.

guided.text: Draw expected waveforms at transformer secondary, bridge output, reservoir capacitor, and regulated output.
For 100 mA load, 1000 uF, and 100 Hz ripple, estimate ripple voltage.
Compare a linear regulator and buck converter for efficiency, dissipation, noise, complexity, and required headroom.
Create a rail table for a board with 12 V input, 5 V, 3.3 V, and 1.2 V rails. Include source, load, tolerance, and one test point each.

questions.prompt: Why can an unplugged power supply remain hazardous?
choices: Unplugging always removes all stored energy instantly.
A disconnected supply cannot contain voltage.
Only its display can retain energy.
questions.explanation: Stored energy must be handled under the relevant safe procedure. These course labs use approved low-voltage sources, not mains repair.

questions.prompt: A full-wave rectifier is fed by 60 Hz AC. Before smoothing, how often do its output peaks repeat?
questions.explanation: Full-wave rectification uses both half-cycles, doubling the ripple frequency.

questions.prompt: In a basic rectifier supply, what does a reservoir capacitor do between charging peaks?
choices: Supplies load current while its voltage falls
Blocks all DC load current by definition
questions.explanation: Its stored energy supports the load between peaks. More load current or less capacitance generally increases ripple.

questions.prompt: What is a regulator intended to maintain within specified limits?
choices: Output voltage as input or load changes
The same temperature under every condition
questions.explanation: Regulation has operating limits, including input headroom, load capability and thermal constraints.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches a switch-mode power supply?
choices: It switches a power device and transfers energy through reactive components.
It relies only on a series resistor for all regulation.
It needs no feedback or control under any circumstances.
questions.explanation: Switching converters use controlled energy transfer. Filtering, regulation and layout still matter.

questions.prompt: A linear regulator drops 12 V to 5 V at 0.20 A. About how much power does it dissipate?
questions.explanation: Correct. (12−5) V × 0.20 A = 1.4 W, which requires thermal evaluation.

pages.title: Gain is an input-to-output ratio with conditions
pages.text: Voltage gain Av = Vout/Vin; current and power gain use their matching quantities. Voltage gain in dB is 20 log10|Av| when impedances/voltage ratios are appropriate; power gain is 10 log10(Pout/Pin). A factor of 10 in voltage is 20 dB, factor of 2 about 6 dB. State sign/phase separately when magnitude dB hides inversion.
pages.remember: Define which quantities, points, and load condition the gain compares.
pages.sourceLesson: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

pages.title: Report gain across frequency and load
pages.text: Record Vin and Vout using the same amplitude convention, frequency, load, supply, and coupling. Calculate ratio and dB. Repeat at a second frequency or load to reveal bandwidth/drive behavior. Automatic scope measurements help, but manual scale and sanity checks protect against measuring noise or a clipped waveform.
pages.remember: A gain number without frequency, load, supply, and waveform quality is incomplete.
pages.sourceLesson: Measure and troubleshoot a signal chain

pages.title: BJT and FET amplifier bias, gain, and power
pages.text: An amplifier stage needs a DC operating point (bias) so the signal can vary without immediately driving the device into cutoff or saturation/clipping. In a common-emitter BJT stage, the base/emitter network establishes current, the collector resistor converts collector-current changes to voltage changes, emitter resistance adds local feedback/stability, and coupling/bypass capacitors shape AC response. Small-signal voltage gain depends on device transconductance and surrounding resistances, while output swing is limited by supply and bias point. In a common-source FET/MOSFET stage, gate bias sets the operating region, drain current changes with gate-source voltage, and drain/source resistances set gain and feedback. For either type, first verify DC terminal voltages and current before calculating/observing AC gain. Power analysis distinguishes signal power from device dissipation: a transistor can meet gain target yet exceed safe dissipation.
pages.sourceLesson: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

pages.title: Operational amplifiers and gain analysis
pages.text: An operational amplifier is a high-gain differential amplifier normally used with feedback so external components define useful behavior. In the ideal negative-feedback model, input currents are approximately zero and feedback drives the two input voltages toward equality while the output remains inside its valid range. An inverting amplifier has gain Av = -Rf/Rin; a non-inverting amplifier has Av = 1 + Rf/Rg. Real op-amps have finite supply rails/output swing, input common-mode range, output-current limit, gain-bandwidth product, slew rate, offset and noise. A mathematically correct gain can therefore fail physically if the required output exceeds the rail, changes too quickly, or drives too heavy a load. Power checks include output/load power and device dissipation/thermal limit, not only gain. Comparator-like open-loop use is different from linear closed-loop operation.
pages.sourceLesson: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

pages.title: Amplifiers use supply energy to reproduce a signal with gain
pages.text: An amplifier does not create energy from the input signal. The input controls how supply power is delivered to the output. Voltage gain is Av=Vout/Vin under stated conditions; current and power gain are distinct quantities. Preamplifiers usually raise small signals before later processing, while line or driver stages interface between blocks or loads. Class A, B, AB, and switching amplifier classes differ in conduction and efficiency/distortion tradeoffs. Frequency response describes how gain and phase change with frequency, so a quoted 'gain of 10' is incomplete without frequency, load, supply, and output-quality conditions.
pages.sourceLesson: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

pages.title: Real amplifiers have rails, bandwidth, drive, and bias limits
pages.text: Output cannot exceed supply-dependent swing or current capability. Gain usually falls with frequency. Input common-mode range, offset, slew rate, noise, and output loading matter. A calculated 5× gain from a 1 V peak input requires a 5 V peak output; on a 5 V single supply that may be impossible without biasing and rail-to-rail capability.
pages.remember: Calculate the requested output, then compare it with supply, common-mode, bandwidth, slew, and load constraints.
pages.sourceLesson: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

pages.title: Op-amp rules are conditional approximations
pages.text: With negative feedback and linear operation, an ideal op-amp model assumes negligible input current and feedback drives the two inputs toward nearly equal voltage. This leads to inverting gain -Rf/Rin and non-inverting gain 1+Rf/Rg. The rules fail when the output saturates, the input common-mode range is exceeded, output current is too high, slew rate or bandwidth is insufficient, or the circuit uses positive feedback/open-loop comparator behavior. Real analysis therefore checks both the algebra and the device limits.
pages.sourceLesson: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

pages.title: Distortion, loading, buffering, and measurement error
pages.text: Distortion means the output is not a scaled/time-shifted version of the intended input. Clipping occurs when output swing reaches a limit; crossover distortion can appear near zero in poorly biased push-pull stages; slew-rate limiting distorts fast/large signals; overload, thermal/current limiting and nonlinear bias can add harmonics or compression. Measurement equipment can create apparent distortion or gain error by loading the circuit. A DMM or scope input has finite resistance and capacitance; a 1× scope probe often loads a high-impedance/high-frequency node more than a 10× probe. Reduce loading by selecting a higher-impedance probe/meter, using a 10× probe when appropriate, buffering the node, measuring at a lower-impedance test point, shortening grounds/leads, and accounting for bandwidth. A clean-looking waveform is not proof of the circuit’s unloaded behavior unless the instrument’s effect is considered.
pages.sourceLesson: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

pages.title: Begin with a signal budget
pages.text: Mark expected DC bias and AC amplitude at input, feedback nodes, output, and load. State supply rails and frequency. A DMM can check bias; a scope checks waveform and phase. If the output clips symmetrically, requested swing may exceed both rails; one-sided clipping may indicate bias/common-mode problems; reduced amplitude only with load points to output drive or loading.
pages.remember: Separate DC operating point from AC signal behavior.
pages.sourceLesson: Measure and troubleshoot a signal chain

pages.title: Negative feedback sets predictable closed-loop behavior
pages.text: For an ideal op amp under negative feedback and not saturated, input currents are approximately zero and the input voltages are approximately equal. An inverting stage has Av = −Rf/Rin; a non-inverting stage has Av = 1 + Rf/Rg; a buffer has gain near one but can isolate impedances. These “ideal rules” are conditional consequences of high open-loop gain and feedback—not universal laws.
pages.remember: Before applying virtual-short rules, verify negative feedback and plausible unsaturated operation.
pages.sourceLesson: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

pages.title: Feedback faults leave recognizable evidence
pages.text: An open feedback path can drive the output to a rail because tiny input differences are amplified open-loop. Wrong resistor ratio gives a stable but incorrect gain. Positive feedback causes latching/oscillation rather than linear control. Verify resistor values and continuity with power off, then compare both input pins and output under safe power.
pages.remember: Do not call every railed output “a bad op amp”; verify feedback polarity and continuity first.
pages.sourceLesson: Measure and troubleshoot a signal chain

pages.title: Amplifier roles, classes, stages, and frequency response
pages.text: An amplifier uses energy from its power supply to produce an output signal that is a controlled version of the input. A preamplifier raises a small sensor/microphone-level signal and often establishes noise/impedance performance; a line amplifier drives an interstage or line-level load; a power amplifier delivers substantial voltage/current to a load such as a speaker or actuator. Class A conducts for the full cycle and is linear but inefficient; Class B devices conduct for roughly half-cycles and can create crossover distortion; Class AB biases devices to overlap and reduce crossover distortion; Class D switches devices and filters the result for high efficiency. Frequency response describes gain versus frequency and therefore the usable bandwidth. A narrow-band amplifier intentionally favors a limited band, while broadband designs maintain useful gain over a much wider span and must control stability, noise and flatness. Gain figures only make sense with stated source/load conditions and frequency.
pages.sourceLesson: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

pages.title: Build a signal budget
pages.text: For each stage, record expected DC bias, AC amplitude, frequency range, source impedance, load, and available headroom. A signal budget makes it possible to recognize whether a measured 200 mV output is wrong or exactly what the stage should produce. In an op-amp chain, include both input nodes, feedback network, output, and supply rails. In a transistor stage, include base/gate bias, emitter/source, collector/drain, and coupling points. This table is your expected-state map before the first probe touches the circuit.
pages.sourceLesson: Measure and troubleshoot a signal chain

pages.title: Use waveform shape to classify faults
pages.text: Symmetric clipping near both rails suggests requested swing exceeds available headroom. One-sided clipping can indicate bad bias or common-mode limitations. A triangular large-signal output at high frequency can indicate slew-rate limiting. Reduced gain only after a load is connected suggests output-drive or loading limits. Oscillation or high-frequency noise can point to unstable feedback, poor decoupling, probe grounding, or layout. A DC output at a rail can result from open feedback, wrong polarity, excessive offset, or saturated input—not automatically a failed op-amp.
pages.sourceLesson: Measure and troubleshoot a signal chain

examples.title: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

detail.problem: An inverting op-amp uses Rin = 10 kΩ, Rf = 47 kΩ, and Vin = 0.20 V. Find ideal output.
steps: Check whether the supply rails and input common-mode permit this result.
Check load and bandwidth before expecting the ideal value physically.
detail.answer: Ideal Vout = −0.94 V.
detail.transfer: If powered from a single 0–5 V supply with no bias, a negative output request will clip near the lower rail.

examples.title: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

detail.problem: A non-inverting op-amp uses Rg=10 kOhm and Rf=40 kOhm with Vin=0.4 V. Supply is 0-5 V and the op-amp can swing only to about 0.2-4.8 V.
steps: Ideal gain=1+40k/10k=5.
Ideal output=0.4*5=2.0 V, inside the stated output range.
If Vin rises to 1.2 V, ideal output would be 6 V, impossible on a 5 V supply.
The real output saturates near its upper swing limit; the virtual-input-equality assumption no longer supports the linear gain equation.
detail.answer: 2.0 V is plausible for 0.4 V input; 6 V is not, so a 1.2 V input would drive the stage into saturation.
detail.meaning: Closed-loop formulas must be checked against supply and operating limits.

examples.title: Measure and troubleshoot a signal chain

detail.problem: A non-inverting stage designed for gain 11 produces the correct low-frequency output, but gain falls and the waveform becomes triangular at high frequency.
steps: Correct low-frequency gain makes resistor ratio/feedback topology plausible.
High-frequency gain loss suggests finite bandwidth.
Triangular output at large amplitude suggests slew-rate limiting.
Reduce amplitude and compare; check datasheet gain-bandwidth and slew rate.
detail.answer: Prioritize bandwidth/slew limitations rather than resistor replacement.
detail.transfer: Changing one condition—amplitude—separates small-signal bandwidth from large-signal slew behavior.

examples.title: Measure and troubleshoot a signal chain

detail.problem: A non-inverting stage should have gain 5. It measures gain 5 at 1 kHz and 100 mV input, but at 100 kHz and 1 V input the output becomes triangular with much lower amplitude.
steps: The low-frequency result supports the resistor ratio and feedback polarity.
High frequency plus large output swing increases required slew rate.
Estimate required sine-wave slew rate 2*pi*f*Vpk and compare with datasheet.
Reduce input amplitude at 100 kHz. If shape improves, slew-rate limitation is supported; if gain remains low, also check gain-bandwidth.
detail.answer: Prioritize slew-rate and bandwidth limits rather than replacing feedback resistors.
detail.meaning: Changing amplitude while holding frequency separates large-signal slew behavior from small-signal bandwidth.

questions.prompt: An ideal inverting op-amp has Rin=1000 Ω, Rf=10000 Ω, and Vin=0.2 V. With the non-inverting input grounded and operation in the linear region, what is Vout?

At equal impedances, a voltage amplitude doubles. What is the approximate gain in dB?
questions.explanation: Use 20 log10(2) for this voltage ratio; power would increase by a factor of four at equal resistance.

questions.prompt: An amplifier's output flattens near its voltage limits as input amplitude increases. What is happening?
choices: A reduction in the source frequency to zero
An increase in ADC bit count
questions.explanation: The demanded output exceeds available swing. Reduce amplitude or redesign within device limits.

questions.prompt: A probe changes the output of a high-impedance amplifier node. What should be investigated?
choices: Probe loading and the node's source impedance
The length of the amplifier's product name
questions.explanation: Input resistance and capacitance load the node. A suitable probe and measurement method can reduce this error.

questions.prompt: An idealized class A output device conducts for how much of a full signal cycle?
choices: Only when the power is switched off
questions.explanation: Class A operation uses conduction throughout the cycle; other classes trade conduction angle, efficiency and distortion.

questions.prompt: An ideal non-inverting op-amp has Rf = 9 kΩ and Rg = 1 kΩ. In linear operation, what is its voltage gain?
questions.explanation: The non-inverting closed-loop gain is 1 + Rf/Rg = 10. Input range and output swing must permit linear operation.

questions.prompt: What does an amplifier's frequency response describe?
choices: How its gain and phase vary with frequency
Only the maximum DC supply voltage
The exact resistance of every cable connected to it
questions.explanation: Frequency response helps determine whether the amplifier can reproduce the intended signal band.

questions.prompt: A voltage gain of 10 corresponds to approximately what dB value?
questions.explanation: Correct. 20 log10(10) = 20 dB.

pages.title: ESD damage can be latent and invisible
pages.text: Static charge can reach damaging voltage without a sensation. Grounded dissipative mats, correctly connected wrist straps, antistatic packaging, controlled handling, and common-point grounding reduce potential differences. A strap is not used for hazardous energized work. ESD control protects components; electrical safety protects people, and the controls must not be confused.
pages.remember: Protect device, person, and process with the right control for each hazard.
pages.sourceLesson: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

pages.title: ESD control is specific to the work state
pages.text: At a suitable de-energized ESD workstation, use approved grounding systems, dissipative surfaces, packaging, and handling practices. An ESD wrist strap is not permission to connect yourself to hazardous energized circuitry. Workmanship control also includes ventilation/fume management, eye protection, hot-tool handling, and lead/solder hygiene. Physical skill claims require physical evidence; a virtual inspection can teach defect recognition but cannot prove hand technique, heat control, or actual joint quality.
pages.sourceLesson: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

pages.title: Physical safety and ESD remain active through rework
pages.text: Power down, discharge through approved method, remove batteries/sources when required, use ventilation/PPE/tool controls, establish ESD protection for sensitive devices, and verify polarity/shorts before repower. Stop/escalate for lifted pads, damaged insulation, unknown high energy, or unavailable proper tooling.
pages.remember: Schedule pressure never changes the stop criteria.
pages.sourceLesson: Retention: workmanship, cabling, measurement, and safety

pages.title: Solder safety, fumes, splatter, flux, and alloy choice
pages.text: Soldering hazards include hot iron tips, molten solder, hot components, splatter, fumes, sharp leads and contamination from lead-bearing alloys. Keep the iron in a stable holder, keep combustibles away, use eye protection where splatter is possible, and treat the work as hot until proven otherwise. Soldering fumes are primarily heated flux decomposition products; local ventilation/fume extraction controls inhalation. Lead exposure is mainly a contamination/ingestion problem from handling lead-bearing solder, so wash hands before eating or touching food and keep the bench clean; do not rely on smoke as an indicator of lead vapor. Flux removes oxides and promotes wetting. Rosin/no-clean/water-soluble chemistries have different process and cleaning requirements; use only material compatible with the assembly and procedure. Solder alloy is chosen by process temperature, reliability, compatibility and environmental requirement. Lead-free alloys generally melt at higher temperatures than traditional tin-lead alloys, so dwell time and thermal damage still require control. Splatter is reduced by clean/dry surfaces, proper tip temperature, correct solder feed and avoiding trapped moisture or excessive flux.
pages.sourceLesson: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

pages.title: Desoldering principles, equipment care, and solder wick
pages.text: Desoldering succeeds when old solder is heated only long enough to reflow and is then removed without prying on a still-bonded lead or overheating the pad. Common tools include a manual spring pump, vacuum desoldering station/gun, hot-air/rework tools for appropriate SMT work, and solder wick. Keep tips clean/tinned, filters/nozzles maintained, and tools at the temperature and airflow specified for the assembly. Solder wick is fine copper braid that uses capillary action to absorb molten solder. Place fresh flux or a small amount of fresh solder when needed to improve heat transfer, lay the wick on the joint, place the iron on top of the wick, allow solder to flow into the braid, then lift iron and wick together before the joint freezes. Use a fresh section for the next removal. Do not scrub the pad, pull while solder is solid, or dwell until the laminate/pad lifts. After removal, inspect the pad/PTH, clean as required and verify the electrical result.
pages.sourceLesson: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

pages.title: Soldering is controlled wetting and heat transfer
pages.text: A sound solder joint requires clean compatible surfaces, enough heat to bring the joint—not just the solder—into the proper temperature range, suitable flux activity, and controlled dwell time. Solder should wet the lead and pad with a smooth fillet appropriate to the connection. Too little heat or movement during solidification can create poor wetting or a disturbed/cold joint; excessive heat can damage pads, insulation, components, or laminate. The goal is not 'make it shiny' because alloy, finish, and process can change appearance. Inspection looks at wetting, geometry, bridging, voids/contamination where visible, lead/pad condition, and electrical verification.
pages.sourceLesson: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

pages.title: Rework controls heat and mechanical stress
pages.text: Select tip, temperature, flux, braid/pump/hot-air method, and support before removal. Do not force a lead while solder is solid or dwell until the pad lifts. Remove residue where required, inspect under magnification, and verify continuity plus absence of shorts. Escalate when pads/traces or multilayer connections exceed your equipment and skill.
pages.remember: The goal is a verified assembly, not merely a removed component.
pages.sourceLesson: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

pages.title: Rework has a damage budget
pages.text: Every heat cycle stresses pads, plated-through holes, components, and laminate. Use the correct tip, temperature/process, flux, solder-wick or vacuum tool, magnification, and mechanical support. Do not pull a lead while solder is solid. Solder wick transfers molten solder into braided copper by capillary action; it works best with clean fluxed braid and controlled heat, not excessive pressure. BGA joints are hidden under the package and generally require controlled rework equipment, thermal profiling, and inspection methods beyond casual hand soldering. Pad/trace repair must restore the intended net and mechanical reliability without creating clearance or high-speed-signal problems.
pages.sourceLesson: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

pages.title: A good joint comes from clean surfaces, correct heat, and wetting
pages.text: Heat both pad and lead, feed suitable solder to the joint, allow wetting, then remove solder and iron without movement while it solidifies. An acceptable joint has proper coverage and contour without bridge, ball, void, disturbed surface, excessive solder, or damaged insulation/pad. Appearance helps, but continuity and functional verification complete the evidence.
pages.remember: Solder follows heat and clean metal; the iron does not paint solder onto a cold joint.
pages.sourceLesson: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

pages.title: Heat shunts, cold joints, and good mechanical/electrical connections
pages.text: Heat-sensitive components can be protected by controlling iron temperature, contact time, thermal mass and, where appropriate, a clip-on heat shunt between the joint and component body. A cold or disturbed solder joint forms when surfaces never reach the proper wetting temperature, are oxidized/contaminated, have inadequate flux, or move while the solder solidifies. It often looks dull, lumpy or poorly flowed, but appearance alone is not enough—inspect wetting and joint geometry and verify function. A good connection begins with sound mechanical placement, clean metallization, correct lead/pad contact, proper heating of the joint (not just the solder), complete wetting, controlled solder amount and no unintended bridges. Electrical quality means low-resistance stable connection without shorts; mechanical quality means the joint is not carrying loads it was never intended to support. Excess heat can lift pads, damage insulation or components and dissolve plating, so “more heat” is not a universal repair.
pages.sourceLesson: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

pages.title: SMT/BGA handling and PCB pad/trace/PTH repair boundaries
pages.text: Surface-mount parts and printed-circuit features are small enough that ESD, contamination, mechanical force and uncontrolled heat can create damage that is difficult to see. Handle boards by edges, use ESD controls, protect gold contacts from oils/abrasion, use suitable magnification and tools, and verify component orientation/polarity. BGA packages place solder joints under the package; inspection/rework normally requires controlled equipment, profiles and trained procedures rather than hand-heating an inaccessible joint. Pad, plated-through-hole and trace repair begins by identifying exactly what has separated or opened, removing damage without enlarging it, restoring the required conductor/land with an approved repair method, anchoring it so normal mechanical load does not pull it free, and inspecting/testing continuity plus isolation from adjacent conductors. A lifted pad is not repaired by bridging randomly to any convenient copper. The repair must preserve the intended net, clearance, mechanical stability and, where relevant, high-frequency behavior.
pages.sourceLesson: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

pages.title: Workmanship criteria are observable, not aesthetic preference
pages.text: Inspect wetting/coverage, bridges, excess/insufficient solder, disturbed joints, pad/trace damage, component orientation, insulation clearance, strain relief, crimp/terminal engagement, pin mapping, and cleanliness as applicable. Then verify continuity, no-short, and function. Use the actual workmanship reference/tool process rather than inventing a “looks good” rule.
pages.remember: Visual criteria + electrical verification + functional requirement.
pages.sourceLesson: Retention: workmanship, cabling, measurement, and safety

pages.title: Workmanship evidence combines inspection and electrical verification
pages.text: A solder joint, crimp, connector, or cable can look acceptable and still be electrically wrong; it can also look cosmetically imperfect but meet the actual acceptance requirement. Use the relevant workmanship criteria, then verify continuity/isolation, pinout, load behavior, or signal integrity as appropriate. Keep physical evidence honest: virtual images can train inspection decisions, but only physical work can prove actual tool handling and joint/crimp quality.
pages.sourceLesson: Retention: workmanship, cabling, measurement, and safety

pages.title: Measurement setup is part of workmanship verification
pages.text: A continuity table should name connector viewpoint/pins and expected mapping. A resistance/voltage reading should name reference and circuit state. Scope captures should record node, probe, scale, time base, and condition. For ESD-sensitive assemblies, the verification process itself must not introduce risk. The test should be strong enough to catch the failure mode: intermittent connections need condition-dependent testing, and high-speed cables may need more than DC continuity.
pages.sourceLesson: Retention: workmanship, cabling, measurement, and safety

examples.title: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

detail.problem: A through-hole joint forms a dull ball around the lead and does not spread over the pad.
steps: This suggests inadequate wetting, contamination, insufficient heat transfer, or movement.
Inspect tip condition, surface cleanliness, flux, temperature, and whether pad and lead were heated together.
Reflow with controlled heat only if the pad is intact and the process is safe.
Inspect, continuity-check, and functionally verify afterward.
detail.answer: Treat the shape as evidence of poor wetting; correct the process, then verify electrically.
detail.transfer: The same diagnostic habit separates symptom from cause in electronics faults.

examples.title: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

detail.problem: A through-hole joint looks dull and has a ring-like boundary around the lead. Continuity is intermittent when the board is flexed slightly.
steps: The symptom supports a mechanically/electrically unreliable joint rather than appearance alone.
Power down and inspect under magnification for incomplete wetting, cracking, contamination, or pad damage.
If rework is appropriate, use flux and controlled heat to fully reflow the joint rather than adding a large solder blob.
After cooling/cleaning, inspect geometry and verify continuity with gentle mechanical stability—without stressing the board.
detail.answer: Treat it as a suspect disturbed/cold or cracked joint, rework with controlled process if permitted, then visually and electrically verify.
detail.meaning: Workmanship acceptance combines observation, process, and verification; shine alone is not a criterion.

examples.title: Make physical changes traceable with Git and lab records

detail.problem: A firmware change and wire rework are both made before a failed test begins passing.
steps: Two variables changed, so root cause is not established.
Record both changes and restore/test one at a time if safe.
Create separate commits/notes for firmware and physical rework.
Repeat the original test and adjacent regression tests at a named revision.
detail.answer: Separate changes and bind verification evidence to an exact hardware/software configuration.
detail.transfer: This is essential when an R&D technician and engineer collaborate across revisions.

examples.title: Make physical changes traceable with Git and lab records

detail.problem: A connector pin is re-crimped after intermittent continuity. The circuit now passes, but there is no record of the original fault or tool/die used.
steps: The passing result is useful but not reproducible evidence of workmanship quality.
Record connector/terminal/wire identity, observed original failure, crimp tool/die setting if available, before/after inspection, pull/continuity evidence, and final test.
Link the record to the correct board/harness revision and any related test script revision.
If using Git, commit the note/test update without credentials or unrelated generated files.
detail.answer: Add configuration, procedure, evidence, and traceability so another technician can understand and reproduce the repair.
detail.meaning: Traceability turns a one-time fix into engineering evidence.

examples.title: Retention: workmanship, cabling, measurement, and safety

detail.problem: After header rework, continuity is correct but the board intermittently resets when the cable moves.
steps: Static continuity does not rule out weak joint, pin retention, strain, or supply dip.
Inspect under magnification and monitor relevant rail/reset while applying only safe controlled movement.
Separate harness, connector, and board joint by substitution or boundary measurement.
Repair confirmed cause; repeat static, movement, and functional tests.
detail.answer: Use mechanical plus time-domain electrical evidence; do not accept continuity alone.
detail.transfer: The case becomes a strong portfolio story when documented honestly from symptom to retest.

guided.text: List the purpose of flux, correct heat transfer, solder wick, magnification, and ESD controls in a rework operation.
Classify three cases: solder bridge between adjacent pads, lifted pad after overheating, and insufficient wetting around a lead. For each, name the likely risk and a safe next action.
Explain why a random jumper wire may be unacceptable for a damaged high-speed PCB trace even if continuity is restored.
Write a good commit message and lab-note entry for replacing a 10 kOhm resistor with the correct 1 kOhm value after diagnosing a divider error.
Given a folder containing source code, oscilloscope PNGs, a password file, build outputs, and a test report, decide what belongs in version control and what should be excluded or handled differently.
Rewrite the sentence 'the solder joint was bad so I fixed it' into observation, interpretation, corrective action, and verification.

teachBack: Explain what creates a reliable solder joint, why solder wick works, what makes BGA/pad repair different from simple through-hole rework, and why ESD/physical-skill claims require real procedures and evidence.

Explain how you would document a real hardware rework so a second technician can reconstruct what was wrong, what changed, what tools/materials were used, and why the final verification is trustworthy. Include Git's role and its limits.
Explain how you would verify a solder or harness repair using both workmanship criteria and electrical evidence, and clearly state what simulation can and cannot prove.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of suitable solder flux?
choices: Remove or limit surface oxides so solder can wet the joint
Make every solder alloy melt at room temperature
Provide permanent mechanical strength by itself
questions.explanation: Flux assists wetting; it does not replace proper heat, compatible materials, or a sound joint.

questions.prompt: A connection was moved while solder solidified. Which defect is a concern?
choices: A disturbed joint with unreliable bonding
A guaranteed increase in conductor strength
questions.explanation: Movement during solidification can damage the joint. Appearance must be judged with the alloy and workmanship criteria, not shininess alone.

questions.prompt: How does solder wick remove molten solder?
choices: Capillary action draws solder into the heated braid.
A battery in the braid reverses current flow.
The braid dissolves copper pads instantly.
It cools solder into powder before removal.
questions.explanation: Fluxed braid takes up molten solder by capillary action; excessive heat or pulling risks pad damage.

questions.prompt: Which combination addresses common soldering exposure routes?
choices: Local fume extraction and handwashing before eating
A fan aimed at another person's face and eating at the bench
Holding the board closer to the nose
questions.explanation: Flux fumes and contamination require controls. Hand hygiene matters particularly when handling lead-bearing material.

questions.prompt: A pad lifts during rework. What should happen before continuing?
choices: Assess damage and use an authorized repair or escalation procedure.
Cover the damage with more solder without inspection.
Keep heating until the pad disappears.
Treat a visual connection as proof of circuit reliability.
questions.explanation: Pad and trace damage can compromise electrical and mechanical integrity. Rework requires an appropriate approved method.

course.title: Number systems and Boolean algebra
course.prerequisites: Binary/decimal/hex, bits/bytes, Boolean operators, De Morgan rules
course.misconceptions: Bit weight starts at 0 instead of 1; truth table is an output measurement

sections.title: Number systems, notation and conversions
sections.teachingSpecification: Define prerequisites; teach concept physically and quantitatively; demonstrate a reasoned worked example with labeled visual and units when applicable.

sections.title: Boolean algebra and simplification
sections.teachingSpecification: Define prerequisites; teach concept physically and quantitatively; demonstrate a reasoned worked example with labeled visual and units when applicable.

objectives.title: Convert binary, decimal, octal, hexadecimal numbers
Explain Boolean algebra and its use in digital circuitry

pages.title: Number bases are different representations of the same value
pages.text: Each binary position has weight 2ⁿ; hexadecimal groups four bits per digit and uses A–F for 10–15. Convert binary to hex by grouping from the radix point in fours. Decimal conversion sums active bit weights. Keep value separate from notation: decimal 13, binary 1101₂, and hex D₁₆ name the same quantity. This fluency later makes register masks and bus data readable.
pages.remember: Write positional weights above the bits instead of guessing from pattern recognition.
pages.sourceLesson: Binary, hexadecimal, gates, and sequential state

pages.title: Binary and hexadecimal are representations, not different values
pages.text: Digital hardware commonly groups information into bits, nibbles, bytes, words, and registers. Binary uses powers of two; hexadecimal compresses four binary bits into one digit. The same value can be written as decimal 182, binary 10110110, or hexadecimal B6. Technicians use hex because register values and bus data become readable without long binary strings. Conversion should be mechanical: use place values for binary/decimal, group binary in fours for hex, and keep leading zeros when bit position matters. A value such as 0x08 is not 'eight bits'; it is the numeric value eight written in hex, with bit 3 set.
pages.sourceLesson: Binary, hexadecimal, gates, and sequential state

pages.title: Logic gates implement conditions
pages.text: NOT inverts; AND requires all asserted; OR requires any asserted; XOR is asserted when inputs differ for two inputs; NAND and NOR invert AND/OR. Boolean algebra describes the same behavior symbolically. Build the truth table systematically for every input combination, evaluate inner operations first, and note active-low bubbles or bars. De Morgan’s laws connect inverted AND/OR forms.
pages.remember: A gate name is not enough—check polarity and the exact number of inputs.
pages.sourceLesson: Binary, hexadecimal, gates, and sequential state

pages.title: Logic gates, truth tables, and flip-flops
pages.text: Digital gates implement Boolean relationships: NOT inverts, AND requires all asserted inputs, OR requires any asserted input, NAND/NOR invert AND/OR, XOR asserts for unequal/odd-parity inputs, and XNOR asserts for equality/even parity. A truth table enumerates every input combination and expected output; for n binary inputs it has 2^n rows. Flip-flops store state rather than responding only to current inputs. An SR latch/flip-flop represents set/reset behavior; D flip-flops capture a data state on a specified clock edge; JK/T types provide related toggle/control behavior. Setup and hold requirements mean data must be stable around the active clock edge. When troubleshooting, distinguish combinational logic (output from present inputs) from sequential logic (output also depends on stored state/clock history).
pages.sourceLesson: Binary, hexadecimal, gates, and sequential state

pages.title: Logic gates implement relationships between electrical states
pages.text: A logic 1 and logic 0 are voltage ranges defined by a logic family, not perfect 5 V and 0 V abstractions. NOT inverts; AND requires all asserted inputs; OR requires at least one; XOR is true when inputs differ for the common two-input case; NAND and NOR invert AND/OR. Truth tables are the safest way to verify behavior. Boolean algebra can simplify expressions, while De Morgan's laws explain why bubbles/inversions can transform AND-like behavior into OR-like forms. The schematic symbol and active-low notation must be read together.
pages.sourceLesson: Binary, hexadecimal, gates, and sequential state

pages.title: Digital displays and microcontrollers
pages.text: Digital display circuitry translates binary/encoded data into visible segments, pixels or characters. A seven-segment display uses individually driven LED segments; common-anode and common-cathode packages require opposite drive polarity, and multiplexing rapidly selects digits while sharing segment lines. Character/LCD/OLED modules may include their own controller and interface, so the technician separates “data sent correctly” from “display power/contrast/backlight/pixel drive works.” A microcontroller integrates a processor core with memory and peripherals such as GPIO, timers, ADC, serial interfaces and debug logic. Simple firmware reads inputs, transforms state and writes outputs using variables, conditions, loops, functions and hardware-register/driver calls. An MCU is not merely a small PC: timing, pin electrical limits, reset/clock configuration and direct hardware state are part of correct programming.
pages.sourceLesson: Binary, hexadecimal, gates, and sequential state

pages.title: Sequential logic adds memory and timing
pages.text: Combinational output depends only on present inputs. Sequential circuits also depend on stored state. Latches and flip-flops store bits; registers group storage; counters step through states; clocks coordinate updates. Setup and hold times define windows around a sampling edge during which input must be stable. Asynchronous set/reset inputs can override normal clocked operation. This timing perspective matters because a truth table alone cannot explain why a circuit sometimes captures the wrong state or misses a short pulse.
pages.sourceLesson: Binary, hexadecimal, gates, and sequential state

pages.title: Bits gain meaning from type and context
pages.text: The same pattern may represent an unsigned number, signed two’s-complement value, character, instruction, address, or flags. Width matters: an 8-bit unsigned value ranges 0–255; fixed-width C types make hardware intent explicit. Endianness determines byte order in multi-byte data, while bit numbering usually labels least-significant bit as bit 0. Never interpret raw memory without type, width, and byte order.
pages.remember: Bits do not label themselves; representation rules give them meaning.
pages.sourceLesson: Computer blocks, representation, memory, and the build path

pages.title: PLC purpose, scan cycle, programming concepts, and languages
pages.text: A programmable logic controller is an industrial controller designed for deterministic I/O control and rugged environments. A basic PLC scan reads inputs, executes the control program, updates outputs and performs communications/diagnostics; exact behavior depends on platform. Ladder logic represents relay-like contacts/coils and is common in industrial work, while function-block, structured-text and other IEC-style languages express the same control intent in different forms. Programming concepts still include variables/tags, Boolean conditions, timers, counters, state, functions, sequence and error handling. Different languages exist because some make discrete control, math/data handling, state machines or reusable algorithms easier to express and maintain. A technician must distinguish a physical input state from a software tag and an output command from actual field voltage/current; forcing a software bit does not prove the field circuit is healthy.
pages.sourceLesson: Computer blocks, representation, memory, and the build path

examples.title: Binary, hexadecimal, gates, and sequential state

detail.problem: Convert binary 1011 0110 to hex and decimal.
steps: Group into nibbles: 1011 and 0110.
1011₂ = B₁₆; 0110₂ = 6₁₆, so B6₁₆.
detail.answer: B6 hex and 182 decimal.
detail.transfer: A register value shown as 0xB6 can be decoded bit-by-bit using the same conversion.

examples.title: Binary, hexadecimal, gates, and sequential state

detail.problem: A register reads 0xB6. Convert it to binary and identify whether bits 7, 5, 3, and 0 are set.
steps: Bit positions from left are 7..0: 1 0 1 1 0 1 1 0.
Bits 7 and 5 are set; bit 3 is 0; bit 0 is 0.
detail.answer: 0xB6=10110110; bits 7 and 5 are set, bits 3 and 0 are clear.
detail.meaning: Hex-to-bit conversion is the basis of register masks and digital bus interpretation.

examples.title: Computer blocks, representation, memory, and the build path

detail.problem: An 8-bit unsigned counter holding 255 is incremented once.
steps: Eight unsigned bits represent 0 through 255.
255 is binary 11111111.
Adding one produces 1 00000000; only eight stored bits remain.
The stored result wraps to 0 in unsigned arithmetic.
detail.answer: 0, due to modulo-256 unsigned wrap.
detail.transfer: A wrapped timer/counter can break comparisons unless rollover is handled intentionally.

examples.title: Computer blocks, representation, memory, and the build path

detail.problem: A small C program compiles each source file successfully but the final build reports 'undefined reference to read_sensor'.
steps: Compilation succeeded, so the syntax in the individual source files is acceptable enough to produce objects.
The undefined reference appears during linking because a required symbol declaration/call exists but the linker cannot find a matching definition in linked objects/libraries.
Check whether the implementation file is included in the build, symbol spelling/signature matches, and the correct library/object is linked.
Do not troubleshoot runtime sensor wiring until an executable image exists.
detail.answer: Treat this as a link-stage dependency/symbol problem, not a runtime hardware failure.
detail.meaning: Identifying the build stage narrows the search space before any code or hardware change.

guided.text: Convert decimal 45 to binary and hex, then convert 0x3C back to binary and decimal.
Build a truth table for Y=(A AND B) OR (NOT C). Verify all eight combinations.
A D flip-flop samples on a rising edge. Explain what setup/hold means and why changing D at the same instant as the clock edge can produce an uncertain result.
Classify five failures as compile, link, load/program, or runtime: syntax error, undefined reference, programmer cannot connect, program hard-faults, missing header declaration warning.
Draw CPU, RAM, flash/nonvolatile storage, and peripheral I/O blocks. Trace what happens from power-up to executing an instruction that reads an input.
Explain a PLC scan using a start/stop input and motor output, then identify what field measurement is needed to prove the output actually energized.

teachBack: Explain how one byte can be written in binary, hex, and decimal, then use a small gate expression and a flip-flop to explain the difference between combinational and sequential logic.
Explain the path from C source file to running executable, then connect that path to CPU, memory, and I/O hardware. Include how a PLC scan differs from assuming software state equals physical output.

questions.prompt: What is the hexadecimal representation of decimal 10?
questions.explanation: 10 decimal = A hexadecimal. Each hex place is a power of 16; A through F represent 10 through 15..

questions.prompt: What is the hexadecimal representation of decimal 18?
questions.explanation: 18 decimal = 12 hexadecimal. Each hex place is a power of 16; A through F represent 10 through 15..

questions.prompt: What is the hexadecimal representation of decimal 25?
questions.explanation: 25 decimal = 19 hexadecimal. Each hex place is a power of 16; A through F represent 10 through 15..

questions.prompt: What is the hexadecimal representation of decimal 42?
questions.explanation: 42 decimal = 2A hexadecimal. Each hex place is a power of 16; A through F represent 10 through 15..

questions.prompt: What is the hexadecimal representation of decimal 63?
questions.explanation: 63 decimal = 3F hexadecimal. Each hex place is a power of 16; A through F represent 10 through 15..

questions.prompt: What is the hexadecimal representation of decimal 85?
questions.explanation: 85 decimal = 55 hexadecimal. Each hex place is a power of 16; A through F represent 10 through 15..

questions.prompt: What is the hexadecimal representation of decimal 127?
questions.explanation: 127 decimal = 7F hexadecimal. Each hex place is a power of 16; A through F represent 10 through 15..

questions.prompt: What is the hexadecimal representation of decimal 170?
questions.explanation: 170 decimal = AA hexadecimal. Each hex place is a power of 16; A through F represent 10 through 15..

questions.prompt: What decimal value does binary 1011 represent?
questions.explanation: Its place values give 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11.

questions.prompt: What is decimal 10 in four-bit binary?
questions.explanation: Correct. 8 + 2 = 10, so bits 3 and 1 are set: 1010.
